scenario: Your company uses a Microsoft Entra ID tenant. You need to let an external guest user manage virtual machines in the resource group rg-compute while following the principle of least privilege. What should you assign?

options.text: The 'Contributor' role at the subscription scope.
options.note: Grants far more than VM management, across the whole subscription.

options.text: The 'Virtual Machine Contributor' role scoped to rg-compute.

options.note: Owner also allows managing role assignments — well beyond least privilege.

options.text: The 'User Access Administrator' role at the resource group scope.
options.note: Manages access to resources, not the VMs themselves.

explanation: Virtual Machine Contributor lets the user manage VMs (but not log in to them, or manage the VNet or storage account they connect to). Scoping it to rg-compute keeps permissions as narrow as possible.

scenario: You must prevent administrators from accidentally deleting the production virtual networks in rg-core-networking. Changes to the networks must still be allowed. What should you configure?

options.note: ReadOnly blocks all changes, and the subscription scope is far too broad.

options.text: A 'CanNotDelete' lock on the rg-core-networking resource group.
A 'ReadOnly' lock on the rg-core-networking resource group.
options.note: ReadOnly blocks modifications, which must still be allowed.

options.text: An Azure Policy with the 'Audit' effect for resource deletions.
options.note: Audit only reports; it never blocks a deletion.

explanation: A CanNotDelete (Delete) lock lets authorized users read and modify resources but blocks deletion. Locks apply to everyone, including Owners, and are inherited by every resource in the group.

scenario: All new storage accounts must allow HTTPS traffic only. Non-compliant creation requests must be rejected at submission time. Which Azure Policy effect should you use?

options.note: Allows the deployment and only flags it as non-compliant.
Turns the policy off entirely.
Deploys a related resource after the fact; it does not block the request.

explanation: The Deny effect evaluates the request during the Resource Manager create/update call and rejects it if it does not comply.

scenario: An administrator must be able to manage user accounts, reset passwords and assign licenses only for users in the European HR department, without tenant-wide admin rights. What should you implement?

options.text: A management group for Europe HR.
options.note: Management groups organize Azure subscriptions (Azure RBAC), not Entra ID users.

options.text: An administrative unit with scoped role assignments
A custom Azure RBAC role at the subscription scope.
options.note: Azure RBAC controls Azure resources, not Entra ID user properties or licenses.

options.text: Microsoft Entra ID Protection user risk policies.
options.note: Risk policies respond to compromised identities; they do not delegate administration.

explanation: Administrative units restrict the scope of Entra ID roles (such as User Administrator or License Administrator) to just the users and groups inside the unit.

scenario: In Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM), activating the Global Administrator role must require approval from a SecOps lead and must expire after 4 hours. Where do you configure this?

options.note: Access reviews periodically recertify who holds a role; they do not govern activation.

options.text: Role settings for the role in PIM
In an Azure RBAC custom role definition.
options.note: Global Administrator is an Entra ID role; custom RBAC definitions do not control PIM activation.
Conditional Access controls sign-in conditions, not PIM approval or duration.

explanation: Each role in PIM has its own role settings: maximum activation duration, required approval and approvers, MFA on activation, justification, and so on.

scenario: You manage 15 subscriptions across three business units. You must apply the same governance policies and access controls to all subscriptions in one department. What should you build?

options.note: Administrative units group Entra ID objects, not subscriptions.
Tags are metadata; they do not enforce policy or access by themselves.
A VM configuration tool, not a governance scope.

explanation: Management groups sit above subscriptions. Policy assignments and RBAC role assignments made at a management group are inherited by every subscription beneath it.

scenario: A custom role must let users read VM properties and restart VMs, but not delete them. You draft the definition below. Which statement about it is correct?

options.text: Delete must be added to NotActions or users will be able to delete VMs.
options.note: Anything not listed in Actions is already excluded. NotActions only subtracts from wildcard Actions.
Restart is a control-plane action; DataActions are for data-plane operations such as reading blob contents.

options.text: NotActions acts as an explicit deny that overrides other role assignments.
options.note: NotActions is not a deny. If another role grants delete, the user can still delete. Use deny assignments or locks for that.

explanation: Azure RBAC is additive: a role grants only what its Actions list (minus NotActions). Listing delete in NotActions is only useful when Actions contains a wildcard such as Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/*.

scenario: You need to transfer billing ownership of an Azure subscription to another billing administrator in your organization. Which kind of role is required?

options.text: Global Administrator in Microsoft Entra ID
options.note: Identity administration does not grant billing ownership.

options.text: A billing role on the billing account
User Access Administrator on the root management group
options.note: Controls Azure RBAC assignments, not billing ownership.
Resource group roles never extend to subscription billing.

explanation: Billing ownership is controlled by billing roles in the billing account (Enterprise Agreement or Microsoft Customer Agreement), which are separate from Azure RBAC and Entra ID roles.

scenario: You are enabling self-service password reset (SSPR) in a hybrid tenant. Passwords reset in the cloud must be written back to on-premises Active Directory. What must be enabled?

options.note: Used for Azure Files/hybrid sign-in, not password writeback.
Without writeback, cloud resets never reach on-premises AD.
Publishes on-premises web apps; it does not sync passwords.

explanation: Password writeback sends SSPR changes back to on-premises AD DS in real time. It works with password hash sync, pass-through authentication, or federation.

scenario: For the GPv2 storage account stcorpdata, blobs not modified for 30 days must move to the Cool tier, and blobs not modified for 180 days must be deleted. What should you use?

options.text: An Azure Function that scans the containers daily.
options.note: Works, but adds code and cost when a native feature exists.

options.text: Blob soft delete with a 180-day retention period.
options.note: Soft delete protects against accidental deletes; it does not tier or expire data.

options.text: Set the account default access tier to Cool.
options.note: Only changes the default for blobs without an explicit tier; nothing is deleted.

explanation: Lifecycle management policies move blobs between Hot, Cool, Cold and Archive or delete them, based on age since creation, modification, or last access.

scenario: A financial app needs storage that stays available if one availability zone fails and whose data is replicated to another region in case the whole primary region is lost. Which redundancy option fits best?

options.note: Three copies in one datacenter; no zone or region protection.
Survives a zone outage but not a regional outage.
Replicates to a second region, but the primary region uses LRS, so a zone outage can affect availability.

explanation: GZRS uses ZRS in the primary region and replicates asynchronously to the paired region. Use RA-GZRS if you also need read access to the secondary. Geo-replication is asynchronous, so a regional failover can lose the most recent writes.

scenario: A partner needs read access to one blob container for 4 hours. You must be able to revoke access before it expires without rotating the storage account keys. What should you create?

options.text: An account SAS with an inline expiry time.
options.note: An ad hoc SAS can only be revoked early by rotating the key that signed it.

options.text: A service SAS with a stored access policy
Share storage account key1 with the partner.
options.note: Gives full control of the entire account.
Exposes the data to everyone and cannot be scoped to one partner.

explanation: A stored access policy holds the SAS start, expiry and permissions on the container. Deleting or editing the policy immediately invalidates every SAS linked to it. (A user delegation SAS is another option; it can be revoked by revoking user delegation keys.)

scenario: You are migrating 10 TB from an on-premises Windows file server to an Azure file share. NTFS permissions must be preserved, and later runs should copy only changed files. Which tool fits best?

options.note: GUI tool; not designed for preserving NTFS ACLs in bulk migrations.
No built-in delta sync and slow for 10 TB.
Not suited to multi-terabyte transfers or ACL preservation.

explanation: AzCopy copies NTFS ACLs with --preserve-permissions and SMB properties (attributes and timestamps) with --preserve-info. For repeat runs, Microsoft suggests azcopy copy with --overwrite ifSourceNewer; azcopy sync also works but isn't fully recommended for Azure Files. Robocopy and Azure File Sync are other common answers for this task.

scenario: VMs in vnet-prod must reach storage account stprod01 over a private IP address, and the account must not be reachable from the public internet. What should you configure?

options.text: A private endpoint, with public network access disabled
An NSG rule on the VM subnet that blocks inbound port 443.
options.note: An NSG on your subnet does not control who can reach the storage account's public endpoint.
Connects on-premises networks; it does not make the account private.
The opposite of the requirement.

explanation: A private endpoint gives the storage account a private IP address from your VNet, so traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone. Disabling public network access closes the public endpoint. Remember to set up private DNS (privatelink.blob.core.windows.net) so the name resolves to the private IP.

scenario: You want to sync several branch office file servers with an Azure file share using Azure File Sync. Which Azure resource must you create first?

options.note: A data integration (ETL) service, not file sync.
Used for backup, not real-time sync.
A global web entry point; unrelated to file sync.

explanation: The Storage Sync Service is the top-level File Sync resource. You register servers to it and create sync groups that link a cloud endpoint (the file share) with server endpoints.

scenario: An administrator accidentally deletes several block blobs. Blob soft delete is enabled with 14-day retention. How do you recover them?

options.text: Restore the whole storage account from Azure Backup.
options.note: Unnecessary and disruptive for individual blobs.

options.text: Undelete them within the retention period.
Re-upload the files from local copies.
options.note: Only needed if no protection were enabled.

options.text: Fail over the account to the secondary region.
options.note: Deletions replicate to the secondary, and failover is for regional outages.

explanation: Soft-deleted blobs stay recoverable until the retention period ends. The Undelete Blob operation restores them. (If blob versioning is also enabled, you restore by promoting a previous version instead.)

scenario: You want to set up object replication from stsource (East US) to stdest (West US). Which prerequisites must be met?

options.text: Versioning on both; change feed on the source

options.note: Object replication is not supported on accounts with hierarchical namespace enabled.

options.text: Customer-managed keys in Key Vault on both accounts.
options.note: Encryption keys are not a prerequisite.

options.text: A legal hold on the source container.
options.note: Immutability is not a prerequisite for object replication.

explanation: Object replication copies block blobs asynchronously. It requires blob versioning on both source and destination accounts, and blob change feed on the source account.

scenario: An Azure VM must write logs to a blob container without any storage keys or secrets in scripts or config files. What is the best approach?

options.text: A managed identity with a Storage Blob Data role
Store the connection string in Key Vault and read it at startup.
options.note: Better than hard-coding, but still a long-lived secret you have to manage and rotate.

options.text: Hard-code a SAS token valid for 5 years.
options.note: A long-lived secret in a script is exactly what you must avoid.
Blob containers are not mounted over SMB (that is Azure Files), and it would still need credentials.

explanation: Managed identities get tokens from Entra ID automatically, so there are no credentials to store or rotate. A data-plane role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor grants write access to blob data.

scenario: You are deploying 3 web-tier VMs and need a 99.99% VM connectivity SLA. The VMs must be in physically separate datacenters (separate power, cooling and networking) within one region. How should you deploy them?

options.text: Put all VMs in a single availability set.
options.note: Availability sets spread VMs across racks in one datacenter (99.95% SLA).

options.text: Deploy one VM in each of availability zones 1, 2 and 3.
Deploy the VMs into different resource groups.
options.note: Resource groups are logical containers with no effect on physical placement.
Places VMs close together for low latency, which reduces fault isolation.

explanation: Availability zones are physically separate locations within a region. Two or more VMs across two or more zones qualify for the 99.99% SLA.

scenario: A VM Scale Set must add instances when average CPU exceeds 75% for 10 minutes and remove instances when it drops below 25%. What should you configure?

options.text: Autoscale rules based on a CPU metric

options.note: Scales by time of day, not by load.
Probes take unhealthy instances out of rotation; they do not change the instance count.
Used for patching, not scaling.

explanation: Azure Monitor autoscale lets you define scale-out and scale-in rules on metrics such as Percentage CPU, with a time window, cooldown and instance limits.

scenario: When a new Windows Server VM is deployed, a PowerShell script must install IIS and configure a website. What is the simplest built-in way to do this?

options.note: Built for ongoing configuration management, and needs more setup than a one-off script.
Enables network diagnostics only.
Collects telemetry; it does not run setup scripts.

explanation: The Custom Script Extension downloads and runs scripts on a VM after provisioning, which is ideal for bootstrap tasks like installing IIS. It can be added in the portal, ARM/Bicep, PowerShell or the CLI.

scenario: A web app on App Service plan asp-prod is slow under load. You change the plan from Standard S1 to Premium v3 P1v3 to get more CPU and memory per instance. What type of scaling is this?

options.note: Scaling out adds more instances.
Not an App Service scaling type.
Distributes traffic across regions; it does not change instance size.

explanation: Scaling up moves the plan to a higher pricing tier with more CPU, memory and features per instance.

scenario: A daily batch job runs a container image for about 15 minutes. You do not want to manage VMs or an orchestrator. What is the most cost-effective option?

options.note: You pay for and maintain cluster nodes that sit idle most of the day.
You still manage VMs and OS images.
An expensive, always-on dedicated environment.

explanation: ACI runs containers on demand and bills per second, with no infrastructure to manage. Set the restart policy to Never or OnFailure for run-to-completion jobs. (Container Apps jobs are another serverless option.)

scenario: You want to resize vm-db01 from Standard_D2s_v3 to Standard_D4s_v3, but the new size is not listed because the current hardware cluster does not support it. What should you do?

options.text: Resize it while running; the change has no downtime.
options.note: Any resize restarts a running VM, and here the size is not even available.

options.text: Stop (deallocate) the VM, resize it, then start it again.
Redeploy the VM to a new subscription.
options.note: Moving subscriptions does not help and is unnecessary.

options.text: Recreate the VM from a snapshot in another region.
options.note: Far more disruptive than needed.

explanation: If the size is not available on the current cluster, the VM must be deallocated first. Once deallocated it can land on any cluster in the region that supports the new size. Plan for downtime.

scenario: An App Service web app must connect to a database that is only reachable inside a virtual network, without exposing the database to the internet. Which App Service feature should you configure?

options.note: Reaches individual host:port endpoints (often on-premises) through a relay agent; not the standard way to reach a VNet.
Affects the inbound hostname only.
Unrelated to network access.

explanation: VNet integration routes outbound traffic from the app into a delegated subnet, so it can reach private IPs and private endpoints. (Private endpoints on the app itself control inbound access.)

scenario: An Azure Automation runbook stops non-production VMs at 7 PM every day. How should the runbook authenticate to Azure?

options.text: With a managed identity of the Automation account
With admin credentials stored in the script
options.note: Hard-coded secrets are a security risk.

options.text: With a personal user account that has MFA disabled
options.note: Weakens security and breaks when the person leaves or the password changes.

options.text: With an SSH key pair on local disk
options.note: SSH keys authenticate to Linux VMs, not to Azure Resource Manager.

explanation: Managed identities (system- or user-assigned) are the recommended way for runbooks to authenticate. Azure Automation Run As accounts were retired in 2023.

scenario: You must encrypt the OS and data disks inside a Windows VM using BitLocker, with keys stored in Azure Key Vault. Which technology provides this?

options.note: Encrypts SQL databases, not VM disks.
Encrypts at the storage layer and is on by default; it does not use BitLocker inside the guest.
Protects data in transit, not disks at rest.

explanation: ADE uses BitLocker (Windows) or DM-Crypt (Linux) inside the guest OS, with keys in Key Vault. Note: Microsoft now recommends encryption at host for new deployments, and ADE is scheduled for retirement in September 2028.

scenario: In Azure Container Apps you want to send 10% of traffic to a new revision and 90% to the stable revision. Which feature handles this?

options.note: Routes between endpoints at the DNS level; Container Apps has this built in per revision.
A connectivity feature, not traffic distribution.
Notify on image pushes; they do not route traffic.

explanation: With the app in multiple-revision mode, you assign traffic weights to each active revision, which enables canary and blue/green releases.

scenario: You set up peering between vnet-hub (10.1.0.0/16) and vnet-spoke1 (10.2.0.0/16) in the same region. VMs in the spoke still cannot reach VMs in the hub. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: VNet peering is disabled by default after creation.
options.note: Peering is active once both links exist.

options.text: Only one side of the peering was created.
VNets in the same region cannot be peered.
options.note: Same-region and cross-region (global) peering are both supported.

explanation: Peering needs a link in each direction. Until both exist, the status is Initiated rather than Connected. (The portal creates both links by default; PowerShell and the CLI do not.)

scenario: All internet-bound traffic from Subnet-Internal must go through a firewall appliance at 10.1.1.4. What should you create and associate with the subnet?

options.text: An NSG with an outbound deny rule
options.note: NSGs allow or deny; they cannot change the next hop.

options.text: A route table with a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the NVA
An application security group for the subnet
options.note: ASGs group NICs for NSG rules; they do not route.
Handles inbound global web traffic, not outbound routing.

explanation: A user-defined route for 0.0.0.0/0 with next hop VirtualAppliance overrides the default internet route and forces traffic through the NVA. The NVA NIC also needs IP forwarding enabled.

scenario: 20 web VMs and 10 database VMs share a subnet. You want an NSG rule that lets the web servers reach the databases on port 1433 without listing individual IP addresses. What should you use?

options.text: Application security groups in the NSG rule

options.note: Routes control paths, not port filtering.

options.text: Move the web servers to another subscription
options.note: Adds complexity and does not filter traffic.

options.text: Assign static public IPs to every VM
options.note: Increases exposure and still needs IP-based rules.

explanation: ASGs group NICs by role so NSG rules can reference the group instead of IPs. New VMs only need to join the ASG to pick up the rules.

scenario: VMs in two peered VNets (vnet-a and vnet-b) must resolve each other by name under the custom domain contoso.internal. What should you create?

options.text: A private DNS zone linked to both VNets
A public Azure DNS zone named contoso.internal
options.note: Public zones are resolved from the internet, not used for internal names.
Hard to maintain and error-prone.
A physical connectivity service; unrelated to DNS.

explanation: Link the private DNS zone to each VNet. Turn on auto-registration on the link(s) so VM records are created and updated automatically.

scenario: A Standard Load Balancer distributes TCP traffic across 4 VMs. Connections from the same client IP must always go to the same backend VM. What should you change?

options.text: Session persistence set to Client IP

options.note: Used for scenarios like SQL Always On listeners; it does not create stickiness.

options.text: Change the distribution algorithm to round robin
options.note: Azure Load Balancer does not offer round robin.

options.text: Shorten the health probe interval to 5 seconds
options.note: Affects failure detection, not client affinity.

explanation: By default the load balancer uses a 5-tuple hash, so a client can land on different VMs. Client IP (2-tuple) or Client IP and protocol (3-tuple) persistence keeps a client on the same VM.

scenario: You need a site-to-site IPsec VPN between your on-premises router and an Azure VNet. Which two Azure resources must you create (besides the connection)?

options.text: A virtual network gateway (VPN type) and a local network gateway
An application gateway and an ExpressRoute circuit
options.note: ExpressRoute is a private circuit, not an IPsec VPN.

options.text: Azure Front Door and Traffic Manager
options.note: Global traffic routing services.

options.text: A NAT gateway and a service endpoint
options.note: Neither builds a VPN tunnel.

explanation: The VPN gateway is the Azure side of the tunnel (in GatewaySubnet). The local network gateway represents your on-premises device: its public IP and address prefixes. A connection resource then links the two.

scenario: What is the key difference between a service endpoint and a private endpoint when connecting to Azure Key Vault?

options.text: Service endpoints keep the public IP; private endpoints add a private IP in your subnet.
A service endpoint requires ExpressRoute; a private endpoint uses the public internet.
options.note: Neither statement is true.

options.text: A private endpoint allows internet access; a service endpoint blocks it.
options.note: Reversed and inaccurate.
They work very differently.

explanation: Service endpoints let the service firewall recognize traffic from your subnet, but the service is still reached on its public IP. Private endpoints create a NIC with a private IP in your VNet, reachable from peered VNets and on-premises too.

scenario: An NSG has inbound rules with the priorities below. Which rule is evaluated first?

options.note: Default rules start at 65000 and are evaluated last.
The highest (last) priority allowed for custom rules.
Evaluated after 100.

explanation: NSG rules are processed from the lowest number to the highest, and processing stops at the first match. Custom rules use priorities 100–4096.

scenario: 50 VMs in a private subnet have no public IPs. They need outbound internet access through a fully managed, scalable service. What should you deploy?

options.text: A NAT gateway on the subnet

options.note: Handles private inbound traffic; no internet egress.
Connects VNets, not the internet.

options.text: Application Gateway v2 with a public frontend
options.note: An inbound layer 7 load balancer.

explanation: NAT Gateway gives every VM in the subnet outbound-only internet access through static public IPs or prefixes. Microsoft recommends explicit outbound methods like this: new VNets created with current API versions use private subnets with no default outbound access, while existing VNets keep their current behavior.

scenario: You need to collect performance counters and Windows event logs from 50 VMs into a Log Analytics workspace. What should you deploy?

options.text: The Azure Monitor Agent and a DCR

options.note: Retired in August 2024.
For network diagnostics only.
Adds VM insights map data and needs a base agent.

explanation: The Azure Monitor Agent replaces the legacy agents. Data collection rules define what to collect (counters, events) and where to send it.

scenario: An alert on VM CPU above 90% for 5 minutes must send an SMS and trigger a Logic App. Which component defines these notifications and actions?

options.note: Stores log data; it does not send notifications.
Defines data collection, not alert actions.
Modifies or suppresses actions on fired alerts; the actions themselves live in an action group.

explanation: Action groups are reusable sets of notifications (email, SMS, push, voice) and actions (Logic Apps, webhooks, Functions, runbooks) that alert rules call.

scenario: You want to quickly check whether an NSG rule blocks traffic from vm-src to vm-dst on port 80, without signing in to either VM. Which Network Watcher tool should you use?

options.note: Records raw traffic, which is slower to analyze and needs the VM extension.
Continuous monitoring over time, not a quick rule check.
Logs traffic after the fact and must already be enabled.

explanation: IP flow verify tests a 5-tuple against the effective security rules and returns allow or deny along with the name of the rule responsible.

scenario: You need daily backups of 10 Azure VMs kept for 30 days. What do you need?

options.text: A Recovery Services vault and a backup policy
A Storage Sync Service and a storage account
options.note: For file sync, not VM backup.

options.text: A Log Analytics workspace and alert rules
options.note: Monitoring only.

options.text: An Azure Compute Gallery and a snapshot script
options.note: A do-it-yourself approach without managed retention.

explanation: Azure Backup stores VM recovery points in a Recovery Services vault. The backup policy sets the schedule and retention. The vault must be in the same region as the VMs.

scenario: You suspect packet loss between an Azure VM and an on-premises database over a VPN. You want continuous automated checks of latency and loss, with a hop-by-hop view. Which Network Watcher feature should you use?

options.note: A one-time NSG rule check.
Diagnoses the gateway and connection on demand; it does not monitor continuously.
Shows network resources, not ongoing performance.

explanation: Connection monitor runs continuous tests between Azure and hybrid endpoints, tracking reachability, round-trip time and packet loss, and shows the path topology.

scenario: You need to count error events by computer over the last 24 hours in a Log Analytics workspace. You write the query below. Which query language is this?
code:
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventLevelName == "Error"
| summarize ErrorCount = count() by Computer

options.note: Used by SQL Server and Azure SQL.
An API query language.
Used to select values in JSON documents.

explanation: Azure Monitor Logs, Log Analytics and Azure Resource Graph all use KQL. The pipe (|), where, ago() and summarize are KQL syntax.

scenario: You need to give an app read-only access to blobs in one container using its Microsoft Entra identity. Which role should you assign at the container scope?

options.note: Reader is a control-plane role and does not grant access to blob data.
Manages the account, and is far broader than needed.
Grants full control, including setting ACLs.

explanation: Storage Blob Data Reader is a data-plane role that grants read access to blob contents. Control-plane roles such as Reader do not.

scenario: The Sales department wants every user whose department attribute is 'Sales' to be added to a security group automatically, and removed when they change departments. What should you create?

options.text: A security group with Assigned membership, updated weekly by an admin.
options.note: Manual membership doesn't react to attribute changes.

options.text: A security group with Dynamic User membership and the rule user.department -eq "Sales".
A Microsoft 365 group with Assigned membership.
options.note: Still manual; the group type doesn't change that.
Administrative units scope admin roles; they don't grant group membership.

explanation: Dynamic membership groups evaluate a rule against user attributes and add or remove members automatically. Dynamic groups require a Microsoft Entra ID P1 (or higher) license.

scenario: You try to add a user manually to the group grp-finance, but the 'Add members' option is unavailable. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: The group is a Microsoft 365 group.
options.note: Microsoft 365 groups support manually assigned members.

options.text: The user is a guest account.
options.note: Guests can be added to assigned groups.
Admins can still manage members of ownerless groups.

explanation: Members of a dynamic group are controlled entirely by the membership rule; you can't add or remove them by hand. Change the rule or the user's attributes instead.

scenario: You assign a Microsoft 365 license to a group so its members get the license automatically. For several members, licensing fails with the error 'Usage location isn't allowed'. What should you do?

options.text: Convert the group to a Microsoft 365 group.
options.note: Group-based licensing works with security groups; the group type isn't the problem.

options.text: Assign the license directly to each user instead.
options.note: Direct assignment fails for the same reason.
Unrelated to licensing.

explanation: Licenses can't be assigned without a valid usage location, because services vary by country. With group-based licensing, users without a usage location inherit the tenant's location, which may not be correct for them. Set each user's Usage location (ideally when the account is created), then reprocess the group.

scenario: You need to create 300 user accounts in Microsoft Entra ID from an HR spreadsheet with the least effort, without writing scripts. What should you use?

options.text: Bulk create in the Entra admin center
Create each user manually in the Entra admin center
options.note: Works, but far more effort than needed.
Synchronizes from on-premises AD; it doesn't import a spreadsheet.
Azure Policy governs Azure resources, not directory users.

explanation: Bulk operations let you download a CSV template, fill it in, and upload it to create, invite or delete users in bulk. PowerShell or Microsoft Graph are alternatives when scripting is acceptable.

scenario: A partner company's consultant needs to access an app in your tenant using their own work account. What should you do?

options.text: Invite them as a guest user (B2B collaboration).
Create a new member account and share the password.
options.note: Creates another identity to manage and loses the partner's own sign-in and MFA.

options.text: Add their domain as a verified custom domain in your tenant.
options.note: You can only verify domains you own.

options.text: Set up Microsoft Entra Connect with the partner's AD.
options.note: Far too heavy for one external user.

explanation: B2B collaboration invites external users as guests. They sign in with their own organization's credentials while you control what they can access in your tenant.

scenario: Users in your tenant are inviting guest users without approval. Only members of the Guest Inviter role and admins should be able to invite guests. Where do you change this?

options.note: Conditional Access controls sign-in, not who can send invitations.

options.text: Azure Policy at the root management group.
options.note: Azure Policy doesn't govern directory invitations.
Sync rules affect on-premises synchronization only.

explanation: External collaboration settings control guest invite restrictions (from 'anyone can invite' down to 'no one'), guest user access level, and allowed or blocked domains.

scenario: Your tenant uses a verified custom domain and syncs users from on-premises AD with Microsoft Entra Connect. The user SSPR policy requires one authentication method. How many methods must administrators provide to reset their own passwords with SSPR?

options.text: One, because admins follow the user SSPR policy
options.note: Admin roles use a separate Microsoft-managed policy, not the user policy.
The admin policy requires two methods, not three.

options.text: None; administrators can never use SSPR
options.note: Admins can use SSPR by default (unless it's explicitly disabled for them).

explanation: Admin roles get a Microsoft-managed reset policy that can't be changed. It's a two-gate policy (two methods, no security questions) when the tenant has a custom domain, syncs with Entra Connect, or is more than 30 days into a trial; otherwise it's one-gate. The user SSPR settings don't apply to admins.

scenario: A user has the Reader role at the subscription scope and the Contributor role on the resource group rg-app. What can the user do with resources in rg-app?

options.text: Only read them, because Reader at the higher scope wins.
options.note: RBAC isn't 'highest scope wins'; permissions are additive.

options.text: Create, modify and delete them, but not assign roles.
Assign roles to other users in rg-app.
options.note: Contributor can't manage role assignments.

options.text: Nothing; conflicting assignments cancel each other.
options.note: Assignments never cancel; Azure RBAC is additive.

explanation: Azure RBAC is additive: the effective permissions are the union of all role assignments at that scope and its parents. In rg-app the user has Contributor; elsewhere in the subscription they have Reader.

scenario: A developer needs to manage role assignments for a single resource group, but must not be able to change any resources in it. Which built-in role is the best fit?

options.note: Owner also grants full control over resources.
Contributor can't assign roles at all.
Reader can't change role assignments.

explanation: Role Based Access Control Administrator and User Access Administrator can manage role assignments without granting resource management. RBAC Administrator also supports conditions that limit which roles can be assigned.

scenario: A Global Administrator can't see any subscriptions in the Azure portal, even though the company has several. What is the quickest way for them to gain access to all subscriptions?

options.text: Elevate access via 'Access management for Azure resources'
Assign themselves Billing Reader on the billing account
options.note: Billing Reader shows billing data, not resources.
Gives access only to the new subscription.

options.text: Enable PIM for the Global Administrator role.
options.note: PIM governs Entra role activation, not Azure resource access.

explanation: Entra roles and Azure RBAC are separate. A Global Administrator can elevate access, which grants User Access Administrator at the root scope (/). They can then assign themselves roles on any subscription. Remove the elevation when done.

scenario: You assign a built-in role and want to confirm what a specific user can actually do on a storage account, including inherited assignments. Where should you look?

options.text: The Activity log of the storage account.
options.note: Shows operations performed, not effective permissions.
Advisor doesn't report access.
Sign-in logs record authentications, not authorization.

explanation: Check access shows all role assignments that apply to a principal at that scope, including those inherited from the resource group, subscription and management groups.

scenario: You create a custom role that you want to assign at the scope of several subscriptions. Which property of the role definition controls where it can be assigned?

options.note: Actions lists permitted operations, not scopes.
Lists data-plane operations.
Subtracts operations from Actions.

explanation: AssignableScopes lists the management groups, subscriptions or resource groups where the custom role is available for assignment.

scenario: An auditor wants to block anyone, including Owners, from deleting a resource group's resources, and you discover a deny assignment would be ideal. How do you create a deny assignment directly?

options.text: Use Access control (IAM) > Deny assignments > Add
options.note: There's no option to add deny assignments yourself.

options.text: You can't; only Azure creates them. Use a lock instead.
Create a custom role with all actions in NotActions.
options.note: NotActions isn't a deny and can be overridden by other roles.

options.text: Assign the Reader role at the root management group.
options.note: Additive roles never take permissions away.

explanation: Deny assignments block actions even if a role grants them, but you can't create them directly: Azure creates and manages them, for example when you set deny settings on a deployment stack. For your own resources, a CanNotDelete lock is the practical way to block deletion.

scenario: Users must only create resources in the East US and West US regions. Requests for other regions must fail. What should you assign at the subscription scope?

options.text: A ReadOnly lock on the subscription.
options.note: Blocks all changes, not just other regions.

options.text: A budget with an alert for other regions.
options.note: Budgets track cost; they never block deployments.

options.text: A tag named 'region' on each resource group.
options.note: Tags don't restrict anything.

explanation: 'Allowed locations' uses the Deny effect to reject resources outside the listed regions. A separate 'Allowed locations for resource groups' policy restricts where the resource groups themselves can be created.

scenario: You assign a policy with the Deny effect that blocks a VM size. Ten VMs of that size already exist. What happens to them?

options.note: Azure Policy never deletes existing resources.
Policy doesn't stop running resources.

options.text: They keep running and are reported as non-compliant.
They are resized automatically to an allowed size.
options.note: Deny doesn't change resources; even Modify can't resize VMs.

explanation: Deny blocks new create or update requests. Existing resources are evaluated and marked non-compliant in the compliance view, but they aren't changed.

scenario: Every resource must have a CostCenter tag with the same value as its resource group. Existing and new resources should be fixed automatically. Which policy effect does this, and what does the assignment need?

options.note: Audit only reports.

options.text: Deny, with a managed identity on the assignment
options.note: Deny blocks requests but can't copy tag values.

options.text: Modify, with a managed identity and a remediation task

options.note: Append can't remediate existing resources and is the legacy option for this.

explanation: Modify can add or replace tags during create/update, and remediation tasks fix existing resources. Both Modify and DeployIfNotExists need a managed identity with the right roles. The built-in 'Inherit a tag from the resource group' policy does exactly this.

scenario: You add a tag Environment=Prod to a resource group. A colleague says the VMs in that group are now tagged too. Is that true?

options.text: Yes, resources always inherit tags from their resource group.
options.note: Tags aren't inherited by default.

options.text: No; use Azure Policy to apply the tag to resources.
Yes, but only for resources created after the tag was added.
options.note: No automatic inheritance at all without policy.

options.text: No, because VMs don't support tags.
options.note: VMs support tags.

explanation: Resources don't inherit tags from resource groups or subscriptions. Policies such as 'Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing' apply them automatically. Cost Management can also use tag inheritance for billing reports.

scenario: You need to apply 12 related security policies to multiple subscriptions and track their compliance as a single unit. What should you create?

options.text: 12 separate policy assignments on each subscription.
options.note: Works, but you can't track or manage them as one unit.

options.text: An initiative assigned at a management group

options.note: RBAC controls who can act, not what configuration is allowed.
Blueprints are being retired; initiatives and template specs replace them.

explanation: An initiative groups multiple policy definitions so you can assign them once, pass shared parameters, and see one combined compliance score. Assigning it at a management group covers all subscriptions below it.

scenario: A policy blocks public IP addresses, but one approved project needs them for 90 days. You want the project's resource group excluded and the exception documented with an expiry date. What should you use?

options.text: Delete the policy assignment for 90 days.
options.note: Removes protection for everyone.

options.text: A policy exemption with an expiry date
A CanNotDelete lock on the resource group.
options.note: Locks don't affect policy evaluation.

options.text: Change the assignment's effect to Disabled for 90 days
options.note: Turns the policy off for the whole scope.

explanation: Exemptions remove a scope from evaluation for a specific assignment. They record a category (Waiver or Mitigated), a description and an optional expiry. An assignment's 'excluded scopes' also works, but has no expiry or justification.

scenario: You assigned a new policy and want to see compliance results now instead of waiting for the next evaluation cycle. What can you do?

options.text: Nothing; you must wait up to 7 days.
options.note: You can trigger a scan on demand.
Unnecessary and destructive.

options.text: Re-assign the policy with enforcement mode set to Default
options.note: Not something you can do.

explanation: Azure Policy evaluates resources on a regular cycle (about every 24 hours) and when resources change. You can also start an on-demand scan with Azure CLI, PowerShell (Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan) or the REST API.

scenario: Administrators can't list the access keys of a storage account, and an app that gets keys via the portal fails. All other read operations work. What is the most likely cause?

options.note: CanNotDelete allows listing keys.

options.text: The storage account is in the Cool tier.
options.note: Access tier doesn't affect key management.

options.text: The firewall is set to 'Selected networks'.
options.note: The firewall affects data access, not management of keys.

explanation: Listing keys is a POST operation (listKeys), which a ReadOnly lock blocks. ReadOnly locks can have side effects like this; for example they also block starting or restarting VMs.

scenario: You try to delete the resource group rg-test, but the operation fails. A CanNotDelete lock exists on one storage account inside it. What must you do?

options.text: Remove the lock first, then delete the resource group.
Use the --force flag on the delete command.
options.note: There's no flag that bypasses locks.

options.text: Delete the resource group from the Activity log.
options.note: The Activity log is read-only.

options.text: Move the subscription to another tenant.
options.note: Unnecessary and doesn't remove locks.

explanation: A lock on any resource in a group prevents deleting the group. Someone with Owner or User Access Administrator (Microsoft.Authorization/locks/delete) must remove the lock first.

scenario: You need to move a VM, its managed disks, NIC and public IP from rg-old to rg-new in the same subscription. What happens during the move?

options.text: The VM is redeployed and gets new IP addresses.
options.note: The move doesn't redeploy the VM.

options.text: Both groups are locked during the move; resource IDs change
The VM must be deleted and recreated in rg-new.
options.note: Moving is supported for VMs and their dependent resources.

options.text: The resources keep their original resource IDs and IP addresses.
options.note: The resource group is part of the ID, so it changes.

explanation: During a move both groups are locked for writes and deletes, though the resources keep running. Afterwards the resource IDs reflect the new group, so update scripts and tools that use IDs. Validate the move first with the portal or 'validate move' API.

scenario: You want to move resources to a subscription in a different Microsoft Entra tenant. What is the main limitation?

options.text: Moves only work within one tenant
All VMs must be stopped and deallocated first
options.note: Not the main limitation; cross-tenant moves aren't supported at all.

options.text: Only storage accounts and VNets can move across tenants
options.note: No resource type moves between tenants this way.
Unrelated.

explanation: Move operations work within one tenant. To change tenants you transfer the whole subscription to the other directory, which removes existing RBAC assignments and can affect managed identities and Key Vault access.

scenario: Your management group hierarchy will reflect regions and business units. What is the maximum depth of management groups below the root?

options.note: The limit is higher.
The limit is lower.
There is a limit.

explanation: A management group tree supports up to six levels of depth, excluding the root level and the subscription level. Each management group and subscription has exactly one parent.

scenario: Leadership wants an email when the monthly Azure spend for a subscription reaches 80% of 20,000 USD, and another when it is forecast to exceed 100%. What should you configure?

options.text: A budget with actual and forecasted alerts
An Azure Monitor metric alert on CPU usage.
options.note: Tracks performance, not spend.

options.text: A spending limit on the subscription
options.note: Spending limits apply only to some offer types and stop resources instead of alerting.

options.text: An Azure Policy with the Audit effect.
options.note: Policy doesn't track cost.

explanation: Budgets track actual and forecasted cost and send alerts to email or action groups when thresholds are hit. Budgets don't stop resources on their own; an action group can start automation if you want that.

scenario: You want recommendations for shutting down or resizing underused VMs to cut costs, based on their actual utilization. Which service gives you this?

options.note: Focuses on security posture.
Reports configuration compliance, not usage.
Network diagnostics only.

explanation: Advisor analyzes usage telemetry and recommends right-sizing or shutting down underused VMs, buying reservations, and removing idle resources.

scenario: A team runs the same three D4s_v5 VMs 24/7 and expects to keep them for three years. What gives the biggest compute discount for this steady workload?

options.note: Spot VMs can be evicted at any time, so they don't suit always-on workloads.

options.text: Auto-shutdown schedules on each VM at night
options.note: They need to run 24/7.

options.text: Moving the VMs to a cheaper resource group
options.note: Resource groups don't affect price.

explanation: Reservations give a large discount in exchange for a 1- or 3-year commitment to a specific size family and region. Savings plans offer flexibility across sizes and regions for a slightly smaller discount.

scenario: You need to activate the PIM eligible role 'Contributor' on a subscription for a 2-hour maintenance window. Which license must the user's tenant have for PIM?

options.note: PIM isn't included in the Free tier.
P1 includes Conditional Access but not PIM.

options.text: Microsoft Entra ID P2 (or Microsoft Entra ID Governance)
No license; PIM is included with every Azure subscription
options.note: PIM requires a premium license.

explanation: Privileged Identity Management, Identity Protection and access reviews require Microsoft Entra ID P2 (or Entra ID Governance). Dynamic groups and Conditional Access need P1.

scenario: Every 90 days, managers must confirm whether guest users still need access to the grp-partners group, and access should be removed automatically if they don't respond. What should you configure?

options.text: A recurring access review with auto-apply
A Conditional Access policy for guests.
options.note: Controls sign-in conditions, not periodic recertification.
Can't ask managers to confirm access.

options.text: A ReadOnly lock on the group.
options.note: Locks apply to Azure resources, not Entra groups.

explanation: Access reviews let owners, managers or the users themselves recertify membership on a schedule. Auto-apply can remove access that is denied or not reviewed. This requires Entra ID P2 or Entra ID Governance.

scenario: You need to create a storage account for premium-performance SMB file shares. Which account kind must you choose?

options.note: Premium GPv2 isn't offered; premium files need their own account kind.
Premium block blobs only; no file shares.
A legacy blob-only kind.

explanation: Premium Azure file shares run on SSD-backed FileStorage accounts. Standard file shares use general-purpose v2 accounts.

scenario: Which name is valid for a new storage account?

options.note: Uppercase letters and hyphens aren't allowed.
Names must be 3–24 characters.
Underscores aren't allowed.

explanation: Storage account names must be 3–24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only, and globally unique because they form part of the endpoint URL (name.blob.core.windows.net).

scenario: You move a 2 GB blob to the Archive tier. A week later a user needs to download it within the next hour. What must you do?

options.text: Download it directly; archived blobs can be read like any other.
options.note: Archived blobs are offline and can't be read.

options.text: Rehydrate it to Hot or Cool with High priority, then download it.
Restore it from blob soft delete.
options.note: The blob isn't deleted, just archived.

options.text: Fail over the account to the secondary region.
options.note: Failover doesn't change a blob's tier.

explanation: Archived blobs are offline. Rehydrate by changing the tier (or copying to a new blob) in Hot, Cool or Cold. Standard priority can take up to 15 hours; High priority usually completes in under an hour for blobs under 10 GB.

scenario: You plan to move older blobs to the Archive tier, but the option isn't available on your storage account. The account uses ZRS. Why?

options.text: Archive isn't supported with ZRS redundancy.

options.note: Archive is a Standard-only tier.
Not a requirement.

options.text: Archive is only available for append blobs.
options.note: Archive applies to block blobs.

explanation: The Archive tier is supported only on LRS, GRS and RA-GRS accounts. Cool and Cold tiers are available with ZRS-based redundancy.

scenario: You delete a blob that was moved to the Cool tier 10 days ago. What charge applies?

options.text: None; Cool has no minimum retention.
options.note: Cool has a minimum retention period.

options.text: An early deletion charge for 20 days
An early deletion charge for 170 days
options.note: 180 days is the Archive minimum.
Rehydration applies to Archive only.

explanation: Cool has a 30-day minimum, Cold 90 days and Archive 180 days. Deleting or moving a blob earlier incurs a prorated early deletion charge.

scenario: Regulations require that audit logs in a container can't be modified or deleted by anyone, including admins, for 7 years. What should you configure?

options.text: Blob soft delete with a 7-year retention.
options.note: Soft delete allows deletion and permanent purge after retention; it doesn't prevent changes.

options.text: A CanNotDelete lock on the storage account
options.note: Locks protect the account resource, not the blob data, and can be removed.
Versions can still be deleted.

explanation: Immutable storage puts blobs in a write-once, read-many (WORM) state. Once a time-based retention policy is locked, the retention period can be extended but not shortened, and blobs can't be changed or deleted until it expires.

scenario: Legal counsel needs blobs related to an ongoing lawsuit kept unchanged until the case ends, with no known end date. Which immutability option fits?

options.text: A time-based retention policy of 10 years.
options.note: There's no known end date, and retention can't be shortened once locked.

options.text: A legal hold on the container or blob versions.
Changing the blobs to the Archive tier.
options.note: Archive doesn't prevent deletion.
Doesn't make data immutable.

explanation: Legal holds keep data immutable until the hold is explicitly cleared, with no fixed period. Holds are identified by tags such as a case ID.

scenario: You want to be able to restore an entire container of block blobs to its state at a specific time in the past 7 days. Which feature should you enable?

options.note: Recovers deleted containers, not earlier states of blobs.
For file shares, not blobs.
Copies blobs to another account; no rollback.

explanation: Point-in-time restore rolls block blobs back to an earlier state. It requires blob versioning, change feed and blob soft delete to be enabled, and the restore window must be shorter than the soft delete retention.

scenario: A container was deleted by mistake. Which feature lets you recover it with its blobs, if it was enabled beforehand?

options.note: Doesn't recover a deleted container.
Versions are deleted along with the container.
The deletion replicates to the secondary.

explanation: Container soft delete keeps deleted containers and their contents for the retention period (1–365 days). Enable it together with blob soft delete and versioning for full data protection.

scenario: Someone deletes an Azure file share. How can you recover it?

options.text: Undelete it from share soft delete.

options.note: Versioning applies to blobs, not file shares.

options.text: Rehydrate it from the Archive tier.
options.note: File shares don't use the Archive tier.

options.text: It can't be recovered under any circumstances.
options.note: Soft delete for shares is enabled by default on new accounts.

explanation: Soft delete for Azure file shares keeps deleted shares (including their snapshots) for the retention period, 7 days by default. Share snapshots and Azure Backup protect against changes to individual files.

scenario: Users need to recover earlier versions of individual files in an Azure file share from the Previous Versions tab in Windows. What should you use?

options.text: Blob versioning on the storage account
options.note: Applies to blob storage only.
Moves or deletes blobs; doesn't apply to file shares.
Blob-only and not for file versions.

explanation: Share snapshots are read-only, point-in-time copies of a file share. They show up in Windows File Explorer as Previous Versions. Azure Backup for file shares schedules and retains them for you.

scenario: Domain-joined Windows clients must access an Azure file share using their on-premises AD DS credentials, with existing NTFS permissions applying. What should you configure?

options.text: The storage account key saved in each client's Credential Manager
options.note: Key-based access gives full share access and ignores per-user permissions.

options.text: A SAS token for each user.
options.note: SMB access doesn't use SAS tokens.
Not supported for Azure Files and insecure.

explanation: Azure Files supports AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services and Microsoft Entra Kerberos (for hybrid identities). Share-level permissions are granted with Azure RBAC roles, and NTFS ACLs then control file and folder access.

scenario: Users authenticate to an Azure file share with their AD identities. A group needs read, write and delete access to files at the share level, but not the ability to change NTFS permissions. Which role should you assign?

options.text: Storage File Data SMB Share Reader
options.note: Read-only.

options.text: Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor
Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor
options.note: Also lets users modify NTFS permissions.
A management-plane role that doesn't grant SMB data access.

explanation: SMB Share Contributor allows read, write and delete. Elevated Contributor adds modifying NTFS ACLs. Reader is read-only. Assign them at the share scope or as a default share-level permission.

scenario: A remote user can't map an Azure file share from home over SMB, but it works from the office. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The user's ISP or home router blocks outbound TCP port 445.
Azure Files only works from inside Azure.
options.note: SMB works from on-premises and the internet when port 445 is open.

options.text: The share is in the Hot tier.
options.note: The tier doesn't affect connectivity.

options.text: SMB 3.x doesn't support encryption over the internet.
options.note: SMB 3.x encrypts in transit, which is why internet access is allowed.

explanation: Many ISPs block port 445. Options include a VPN (point-to-site or site-to-site), ExpressRoute, Azure File Sync to a local server, or SMB over QUIC.

scenario: Branch file servers sync with an Azure file share using Azure File Sync, but local disk space is running out. Infrequently used files should stay available but only use space in Azure. What should you enable?

options.text: Cloud tiering on the server endpoint
Lifecycle management on the storage account
options.note: Lifecycle rules apply to blobs, not File Sync servers.

options.text: Blob versioning on the storage account
options.note: Not related to File Sync.
Doesn't free local space.

explanation: Cloud tiering keeps frequently accessed files cached locally and replaces cold files with pointers. They're recalled from Azure on access. You set a volume free-space policy and an optional date policy.

scenario: You create an Azure File Sync sync group. How many cloud endpoints can the sync group contain?

options.note: Only one cloud endpoint is allowed.
Only one cloud endpoint is allowed.

options.text: None; only server endpoints are used
options.note: Every sync group needs a cloud endpoint (an Azure file share).

explanation: A sync group has one cloud endpoint (an Azure file share) and one or more server endpoints (paths on registered servers). A server can be registered with only one Storage Sync Service at a time.

scenario: You need to transfer 70 TB of data from an office with a slow internet connection to Azure Blob storage within two weeks. What should you use?

options.note: Too slow over a constrained link.
Also limited by the slow link.
Syncs over the network and isn't meant for bulk one-time loads.

explanation: Data Box is a ruggedized appliance (about 80 TB usable) that you load locally and ship to Microsoft for upload. Data Box Disk suits smaller volumes (up to about 35 TB per order) and Data Box Heavy suits hundreds of terabytes.

scenario: You want storage account encryption to use keys that your organization controls and can revoke. What must the Key Vault have enabled to store the customer-managed key?

options.text: Public network access from all networks
options.note: Not required; firewalls with trusted services work.
Standard vaults work; HSM-backed keys are optional.
Either access model works.

explanation: Key Vaults (or Managed HSMs) used for customer-managed keys must have soft delete and purge protection enabled, so the key can't be lost by accident. The storage account accesses the key with a managed identity.

scenario: Compliance requires a second layer of encryption for data at rest in a new storage account, using a different algorithm and key. When must this be enabled?

options.text: Any time after creation from the Encryption blade.
options.note: Infrastructure encryption can't be enabled on an existing account.
Not related to performance tier.
Works with Microsoft-managed keys too.

explanation: Infrastructure encryption adds double encryption at the infrastructure level. It must be enabled when the account is created, or through an encryption scope created with it.

scenario: An app signs SAS tokens with Microsoft Entra credentials instead of the account key, so access can be revoked without rotating keys and is tied to an identity. Which SAS type is this?

options.note: Signed with the account key.
Signed with the account key.
A service SAS associated with a policy; still key-signed.

explanation: A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key obtained via Microsoft Entra ID. It works for Blob storage (and Data Lake). The delegation key is valid for up to 7 days.

scenario: Security policy requires that all requests to a storage account be authorized with Microsoft Entra ID; access keys and key-signed SAS tokens must stop working. What should you configure?

options.note: Rotation only replaces keys; they still work.
Enforces HTTPS, not the authorization method.
Locks affect management operations, not data authorization.

explanation: Disallowing Shared Key authorization blocks both account keys and SAS tokens signed with them. User delegation SAS and Entra ID (OAuth) continue to work. Check that your apps and tools support Entra authentication first.

scenario: You need to rotate storage account keys without downtime for apps that use them. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Regenerate both keys at the same time during a maintenance window
options.note: Breaks every app immediately.

options.text: Switch apps to key2, regenerate key1, then repeat
Delete the storage account and recreate it.
options.note: Destroys data.
Unrelated to keys.

explanation: Two keys exist so you can rotate without downtime. Better still, store keys in Key Vault with automatic rotation, or avoid keys altogether with managed identities and Entra authorization.

scenario: The storage account firewall allows only selected networks. Azure Backup and Azure Monitor diagnostic logs must still be able to write to the account. What should you enable?

options.note: Opens data to the public.

options.text: A service endpoint for each Azure region the services run in
options.note: Not possible and not needed.
Defeats the purpose of the firewall.

explanation: The trusted Microsoft services exception lets specific Azure services (such as Azure Backup, Monitor, Event Grid and Site Recovery) reach the account despite the network rules. Resource instance rules allow specific resources.

scenario: You need to host a static marketing website (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) directly from a storage account. Where must the files be uploaded after you enable static website hosting?

options.note: The service only serves from $web.
Static websites are served from blob storage.

options.text: The root of the storage account
options.note: Files must be in the $web container.

explanation: Enabling static website hosting creates the $web container and a web endpoint (name.zN.web.core.windows.net). You set an index document and an optional error document.

scenario: An app reads data from an RA-GRS storage account. The primary region is unavailable. Which endpoint should the app use to keep reading data?

options.note: Not a valid endpoint.
The suffix is appended to the account name, not prefixed.

options.text: Reading isn't possible until a failover
options.note: RA-GRS provides read access to the secondary at all times.

explanation: Read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS and RA-GZRS) exposes a read-only secondary endpoint with the -secondary suffix. Writes need the primary, or a failover.

scenario: You need to copy 2 TB of blobs from one storage account to another in a different region as fast as possible, without the data passing through your workstation. What should you do?

options.text: Download with Storage Explorer, then upload.
options.note: Data travels through your machine.

options.text: Run azcopy copy between the two account URLs.

options.note: File Sync works with file shares and servers.
Uploads from your machine only.

explanation: AzCopy uses the Put Block From URL API to copy directly between accounts, so the data moves service-to-service. Authorize with SAS tokens or Entra ID.

scenario: You want to find blobs across containers by custom attributes such as project=apollo and status=final, and use those attributes in lifecycle rules. What should you use?

options.note: Metadata isn't indexed for querying across containers.

options.text: Resource tags on the storage account
options.note: Apply to the account, not individual blobs.
Not queryable as key-value pairs.

explanation: Blob index tags are key-value attributes that are indexed so you can query blobs across an account (Find Blobs by Tags). Lifecycle management rules can also filter on them.

scenario: Which operation is allowed while a storage account has a CanNotDelete lock?

options.note: Blocked by the lock.

options.text: Uploading and deleting blobs inside containers
Deleting the resource group that contains it
options.note: Blocked because of the locked resource.

options.text: Removing the lock without the right permissions
options.note: Requires Owner or User Access Administrator.

explanation: Locks apply to the management plane (the resource itself). Data plane operations like uploading or deleting blobs aren't blocked; use immutability policies and soft delete to protect the data.

scenario: You configure a lifecycle rule to delete blobs 90 days after creation, but some blobs are still there after 100 days. Which is a possible explanation?

options.text: New or changed policies can take up to 24 hours to take effect
Lifecycle rules only run on Premium block blob accounts
options.note: They work on GPv2, Blob storage and Premium block blob accounts.
No such requirement.

options.text: Delete isn't a supported lifecycle action.
options.note: Delete is supported.

explanation: After you create or change a lifecycle policy, it can take up to 24 hours before it takes effect and the first run starts, and large accounts can take longer to process. Also check the rule's filters (prefix, blob type, index tags) and whether the blobs are under an immutability policy, which blocks deletion.

scenario: You need to convert an existing storage account from LRS to GRS. What is true?

options.text: Change the redundancy setting in place
Create a new GRS account and copy the data with AzCopy
options.note: Not required for LRS to GRS; the setting can be changed in place.

options.text: GRS is only available for Premium accounts.
options.note: GRS is a Standard-tier option.

options.text: Conversion requires deleting all blobs first.
options.note: Data stays in place.

explanation: Switching between LRS, GRS and RA-GRS is done in the account's Redundancy settings. Changes involving zone redundancy (to ZRS or GZRS) use a conversion process and may have extra requirements.

scenario: You deploy an ARM template to rg-web using Complete mode. The resource group contains a storage account that isn't defined in the template. What happens to it?

options.note: That's Incremental mode behavior.

options.text: The deployment fails with a validation error.
options.note: Complete mode doesn't fail because of extra resources.

options.text: It's moved to a new resource group.
options.note: Deployments never move resources.

explanation: Complete mode makes the resource group match the template, deleting resources that aren't in it (subject to locks). Incremental mode, the default, leaves resources not in the template alone.

scenario: Before deploying a modified Bicep file to production, you want to preview which resources will be created, changed or deleted without making any changes. What should you run?

options.note: Validate checks syntax and some rules, but doesn't show resource-level changes.
Exports the current state; no comparison.
Compiles Bicep to JSON; no comparison with Azure.

explanation: The what-if operation compares the template against the current state and lists creates, modifies, deletes and ignores. PowerShell has New-AzResourceGroupDeployment -WhatIf.

scenario: You have an existing ARM JSON template and want to convert it to Bicep for easier maintenance. What should you use?

options.note: Build goes the other way: Bicep to JSON.
The syntax is different.
Moves resources between regions.

explanation: decompile does a best-effort conversion of ARM JSON to Bicep. Review the output, since some expressions may need manual cleanup.

scenario: A template parameter must receive an admin password from Azure Key Vault at deployment time, without the password appearing in the parameter file. What must the Key Vault allow?

options.text: Access for Azure Resource Manager template deployment
Public network access from all networks on the secret
options.note: Never expose secrets publicly.

options.text: Access for Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption
options.note: That setting is for ADE, not deployments.

options.text: A ReadOnly lock on the vault.
options.note: Locks don't grant access.

explanation: A parameter file can reference a Key Vault secret (keyVault id plus secretName). Resource Manager retrieves it during deployment if the vault allows template deployment and the deploying user has permission on the vault.

scenario: You need to reuse the template that created a resource group's current resources as a starting point for a new environment. What is the quickest way to get it?

options.text: Export template on the resource group
Download the JSON from the Activity log's deployment entries
options.note: Lists operations, not templates.
Advisor doesn't generate templates.
Runs scripts inside VMs.

explanation: Export template generates an ARM/Bicep template from existing resources. The output often needs cleanup (hard-coded values, unsupported types) before reuse.

scenario: Which ARM template section declares values that are computed once and reused within the template, such as a combined storage account name?

options.note: Parameters are provided at deployment time.
Outputs return values after deployment.
Declares the resources to deploy.

explanation: Variables hold values built from parameters, functions or constants (for example concat or uniqueString), so expressions aren't repeated throughout the template.

scenario: You need to sign in to Azure VMs over RDP and SSH from the Azure portal, without public IP addresses on the VMs and without a VPN. What should you deploy?

options.text: Azure Bastion in the virtual network
A public load balancer with inbound NAT rules
options.note: Exposes RDP and SSH to the internet.
Outbound only.
For HTTP(S) apps, not RDP/SSH.

explanation: Azure Bastion provides browser-based (or native client) RDP and SSH over TLS. It's deployed into a dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet, which must be /26 or larger.

scenario: You're deploying Azure Bastion. Which subnet configuration is required?

options.note: Wrong name and too small.
Reserved for VPN and ExpressRoute gateways.

options.text: Any subnet, as long as it has an NSG
options.note: The name and size are mandatory.

explanation: Bastion needs a dedicated subnet with that exact name, /26 or larger, and no other resources in it. The exception is the Bastion Developer SKU, which needs neither a dedicated subnet nor a public IP.

scenario: A VM stopped responding and you can't connect over RDP. You want to see a screenshot of its console to check whether it's stuck at boot. What must be enabled?

options.note: Doesn't give a console view.
Network performance only.
Doesn't help when the OS is stuck.

explanation: Boot diagnostics captures the console screenshot and serial log. Serial console, which gives interactive text access, also requires boot diagnostics.

scenario: You need to reset the local administrator password on a Windows VM that you can't sign in to. What is the simplest built-in method?

options.text: Use 'Reset password' in the portal (VMAccess extension).
Delete the VM and recreate it from the OS disk.
options.note: Far more disruptive.
Diagnostic only.
Doesn't change credentials.

explanation: Reset password uses the VMAccess extension through the VM agent to reset the local admin password or SSH key, and can also reset the RDP configuration.

scenario: You need to run a PowerShell script inside a VM to collect diagnostics. The VM has no inbound network access. What should you use?

options.note: Needs network reachability to the VM.
Tests NSG rules; doesn't run scripts.
Interactive and not designed for running scripts.

explanation: Run command executes scripts through the VM agent over the Azure control plane, so no network access to the VM is needed.

scenario: You redeploy a VM to fix a host-related issue. What happens to data on the VM's temporary disk (D: on Windows)?

options.note: The temporary disk is local to the host.

options.text: It's moved to the OS disk.
options.note: Never happens automatically.

options.text: It's backed up automatically to a storage account.
options.note: No automatic backup.

explanation: Redeploy moves the VM to a new host and restarts it. The temporary disk is on the old host's local storage, so its contents are lost, just as when the VM is deallocated.

scenario: You create a Windows VM image to deploy many identical VMs. What must you do before capturing a generalized image?

options.note: Not required to capture an image.
Encrypted VMs complicate imaging.
Not required.

explanation: Sysprep removes machine-specific information so each VM from the image is unique. After capture, the source VM is marked generalized and can't be started again. Linux uses waagent -deprovision.

scenario: You need to share VM images with other subscriptions in your tenant and replicate them to several regions with versioning. What should you use?

options.note: No built-in versioning, regional replication or sharing model.
For container images.
Templates describe resources, not disk images.

explanation: Azure Compute Gallery stores image definitions and versions, replicates them across regions, and shares them through RBAC, direct sharing or community galleries.

scenario: You need to run a batch workload on the cheapest VMs possible. The workload can tolerate interruptions. What should you use, and what can happen?

options.text: Spot VMs; they can be evicted with 30 seconds' notice.
Reserved instances; they may be paused at night.
options.note: Reservations don't pause VMs.

options.text: B-series VMs; they're guaranteed never to be interrupted.
options.note: Burstable VMs are a size family, not a pricing model.

options.text: Dedicated hosts; they're the cheapest option.
options.note: Dedicated hosts cost more.

explanation: Spot VMs use spare capacity at a deep discount. You set an eviction policy (Deallocate or Delete) and an optional maximum price.

scenario: You need the highest-performance managed disk for a database's log files, with sub-millisecond latency and IOPS adjustable without downtime. Which disk type fits, and what is one limitation?

options.text: Ultra Disk; it can't be used as an OS disk.
Standard HDD; it doesn't support snapshots.
options.note: Standard HDD is the lowest-performance tier.

options.text: Premium SSD; it can't be resized.
options.note: Premium SSDs can be resized.

options.text: Standard SSD; it can't be attached to VMs.
options.note: Standard SSDs attach to VMs.

explanation: Ultra Disks (and Premium SSD v2) offer adjustable IOPS and throughput with very low latency. They're data disks only. Use Premium SSD or Standard SSD for the OS disk.

scenario: You need to decrease the size of a 512 GiB managed data disk to 256 GiB. What is true?

options.text: You can shrink it in the portal after stopping the VM.
options.note: Managed disks can't be shrunk.

options.text: You can't shrink it; create a new disk and copy the data.
Shrinking happens automatically if the disk is mostly empty.
options.note: Disks don't auto-shrink.

options.text: Change the disk type to Standard HDD to shrink it.
options.note: Changing type doesn't change size.

explanation: Azure supports expanding managed disks, but not reducing their size. To get a smaller disk, create a new disk and migrate the data.

scenario: You want to move a running VM and its dependencies from East US to West Europe with minimal manual work. Which service is designed for this?

options.note: Moving a resource group doesn't change the region of its resources.
Connectivity only.
Governs configuration; doesn't move resources.

explanation: Resource Mover orchestrates moving resources across regions, including dependencies such as VNets and NSGs. It uses Site Recovery replication for VMs. Moving within a region (between resource groups or subscriptions) doesn't change location.

scenario: Your web app on App Service needs a staging environment where you can test new releases and then swap into production with no downtime. Which App Service plan tier is the minimum?

options.note: No deployment slots.
No deployment slots.
No deployment slots.

explanation: Deployment slots require Standard or higher (Standard has 5 slots, Premium 20). A swap warms up the staging slot and then switches routing, so there's no downtime.

scenario: After a slot swap, production started using the staging database connection string. The connection string should always stay with its slot. What should you configure?

options.text: Mark it as a deployment slot setting.
Store it in the web.config only.
options.note: Config files move with the deployed code.

options.text: Use a different App Service plan for staging.
options.note: Doesn't control what moves during a swap.
Doesn't stop settings from swapping.

explanation: Settings marked as deployment slot settings (sticky) stay with their slot during a swap. Unmarked app settings and connection strings move with the app.
