scenario: You need an App Service web app to scale out automatically based on CPU load. What is the minimum App Service plan tier for autoscale?

options.note: No scale-out.
Basic supports manual scale-out only (up to 3 instances).
Runs on shared infrastructure without scaling.

explanation: Rule-based autoscale requires Standard or higher. Premium v3 also supports automatic scaling based on HTTP traffic.

scenario: Three web apps share one App Service plan. You scale the plan up from S1 to P1v3. What is affected?

options.text: Only the first app in the plan.
options.note: The plan's resources are shared by all apps.

options.text: All three apps, since they run on the plan's instances.
None of them until each app is restarted manually.
options.note: The change applies automatically.
All apps in the plan are affected.

explanation: Apps in the same plan share its VM instances, so scaling up or out applies to every app in the plan. Put an app in its own plan if it needs independent scaling.

scenario: You need to bind a custom domain with a TLS/SSL certificate to an App Service web app. What is the minimum pricing tier?

options.note: Doesn't support custom domains.
Works, but Basic is enough.
Works, but Basic is enough.

explanation: Custom domains with TLS bindings require Basic or higher. You also prove domain ownership with a CNAME or A record plus a TXT verification record.

scenario: You want container images in Azure Container Registry to be replicated to registries in three regions, so nearby deployments pull them quickly. Which ACR tier is required?

options.note: No geo-replication.
No geo-replication.

options.text: Any tier, with a lifecycle rule
options.note: Lifecycle rules don't replicate registries.

explanation: Geo-replication is a Premium feature, as are private endpoints (Private Link). Images are pushed once and replicated to all configured regions.

scenario: An ACI deployment needs a web container plus a logging sidecar that share the same IP address, lifecycle and local network. How should you deploy them?

options.text: As two containers in one container group.
As two separate container groups with VNet peering.
options.note: Separate groups don't share an IP or lifecycle.
Not ACI.
Not containers.

explanation: A container group is ACI's top-level resource. Containers in a group run on the same host and share network, storage volumes and lifecycle. Multi-container groups are supported on Linux.

scenario: Data written by an Azure Container Instances container must survive restarts and be shared with other services. What should you mount?

options.text: An Azure file share as a volume

options.note: Lost when the container restarts.
Shared within the group, but not persistent beyond its lifetime.
Clones a repo at startup; it isn't persistent storage.

explanation: ACI can mount Azure Files shares as volumes for persistent, shareable storage. Provide the storage account name, share name and key in the volume definition.

scenario: A containerized API on Azure Container Apps gets no traffic overnight. You want to pay nothing for compute when idle and scale up automatically on HTTP requests. What should you configure?

options.text: Min replicas 0 with an HTTP scale rule
Min replicas 3 with a CPU scale rule
options.note: Keeps replicas running all night.
Plans are billed while they exist.
Breaks the app and doesn't affect scaling costs.

explanation: Container Apps uses KEDA-based scale rules (HTTP, TCP, queue length, custom). With min replicas at 0, the app scales to zero and starts again when requests arrive.

scenario: Pods in an AKS cluster are stuck in Pending because the nodes are out of CPU. You want the cluster to add nodes automatically when pods can't be scheduled. What should you enable?

options.text: The cluster autoscaler on the node pool

options.note: HPA adds pods, which then stay Pending with no capacity.

options.text: A VM Scale Set autoscale rule outside AKS
options.note: AKS manages its node pools; use the cluster autoscaler.
Unrelated to capacity.

explanation: The cluster autoscaler adds nodes when pods can't be scheduled and removes underused nodes, within the min/max counts you set. HPA scales pod replicas based on metrics; they're often used together.

scenario: You need to add GPU-enabled nodes to an existing AKS cluster for a machine learning workload, without changing the existing nodes. What should you do?

options.text: Add a new user node pool with a GPU VM size.
Resize all nodes in the system node pool to GPU sizes.
options.note: Changes existing nodes and wastes GPU capacity.

options.text: Create a new cluster for every model.
options.note: Unnecessary overhead.
Adds more nodes of the same size.

explanation: Node pools let a cluster mix VM sizes and OS types. Use taints and tolerations or node selectors to schedule GPU workloads onto the GPU pool.

scenario: A VM Scale Set must mix Spot and regular VMs, and allow different VM sizes in the same set. Which orchestration mode should you use?

options.note: Uniform uses identical instances from one model.
Not a scale set orchestration mode.
Controls placement, not orchestration.

explanation: Flexible orchestration manages standard Azure VMs. It supports mixing Spot and on-demand instances and multiple VM sizes, and spreads VMs across zones or fault domains. It's the recommended mode for new scale sets.

scenario: You need to run 10 VMs that can tolerate one physical rack failing, in a region without availability zones. What should you use?

options.text: A single large VM with Premium SSD disks
options.note: One VM can't survive a rack failure.
Packs VMs close together.
Locks don't affect physical placement.

explanation: Availability sets spread VMs across fault domains (separate racks with their own power and network) and update domains (staggered maintenance). That gives a 99.95% SLA.

scenario: You create a subnet with the prefix 10.0.1.0/24. How many IP addresses can you assign to VMs and other resources in it?

options.note: Azure reserves some addresses in every subnet.
Azure reserves more than just the network and broadcast addresses.
Azure reserves exactly 5 addresses.

explanation: Azure reserves 5 addresses per subnet: the network address, the default gateway (.1), two for Azure DNS (.2 and .3), and the broadcast address. A /24 therefore has 251 usable addresses.

scenario: What is the smallest subnet size Azure supports for a virtual network subnet?

options.note: Too small; Azure needs 5 reserved addresses.
Valid, but not the smallest.
A single address.

explanation: /29 is the smallest supported subnet (8 addresses, 3 usable after the 5 reserved). Some services require larger subnets, such as /26 for Bastion and Azure Firewall, and /27 or larger for gateways.

scenario: A VNet uses 10.0.0.0/16. You need to peer it with another VNet that uses 10.0.128.0/17. What will happen?

options.note: The ranges overlap.

options.text: Peering fails because the address spaces overlap.
Peering works, but only for UDP traffic.
options.note: No such restriction exists.

options.text: Peering works only if both VNets are in the same region.
options.note: The overlap blocks peering in any region.

explanation: 10.0.128.0/17 falls inside 10.0.0.0/16. Peered VNets can't have overlapping address spaces, so plan your IP ranges before connecting networks.

scenario: VNet A is peered with VNet B, and VNet B is peered with VNet C. VMs in A can't reach VMs in C. Why?

options.text: Peering supports only two VNets per subscription.
options.note: There's no such limit.
Not required.

options.text: The VNets must be in different regions.
options.note: Region doesn't matter.

explanation: Peering connects only the two VNets in the pair. To reach C from A, peer A and C directly, or route through a hub with an NVA or Azure Firewall (using UDRs), or use Azure Virtual WAN.

scenario: Spoke VNets peered with a hub VNet must use the hub's VPN gateway to reach on-premises networks. Which peering settings are required?

options.text: Hub: Allow gateway transit; spokes: Use remote gateways
Hub and spokes: Use remote gateways
options.note: Only the spoke uses the remote gateway; the hub allows transit.

options.text: Deploy a VPN gateway in every spoke.
options.note: Works, but defeats the purpose of a shared hub gateway.

options.text: Hub and spokes: Allow forwarded traffic only
options.note: Not enough on its own to use the gateway.

explanation: Gateway transit lets peered VNets share one VPN or ExpressRoute gateway. A spoke that uses remote gateways can't have its own gateway.

scenario: Two NSGs apply to a VM: one on its subnet and one on its NIC. The subnet NSG allows inbound TCP 443, and the NIC NSG has only the default rules. Can clients reach the VM on port 443 from the internet?

options.text: Yes, because the subnet NSG allows it.
options.note: Inbound traffic must be allowed by both NSGs.

options.text: No, the NIC NSG's default DenyAllInBound blocks it.
Yes, NIC NSGs are ignored when a subnet NSG exists.
options.note: Both are evaluated.

options.text: Only if accelerated networking is enabled.
options.note: Unrelated.

explanation: For inbound traffic Azure evaluates the subnet NSG first, then the NIC NSG, and both must allow the traffic. Outbound is evaluated NIC first, then subnet. Use Effective security rules to see the combined result.

scenario: Which default inbound NSG rule allows health probes from Azure Load Balancer to reach backend VMs?

options.note: Covers traffic inside the virtual network.
Denies traffic.
There's no such default rule.

explanation: The default inbound rules are AllowVnetInBound (65000), AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound (65001) and DenyAllInBound (65500). You can override them with higher-priority custom rules but can't delete them.

scenario: You need an NSG rule that allows outbound traffic from VMs to Azure Storage in any region, without maintaining IP lists. What should you use as the destination?

options.note: ASGs group your own VM NICs, not Azure services.
Far broader than needed.
Allows everything.

explanation: Service tags represent groups of IP prefixes for Azure services, maintained by Microsoft. Regional variants such as Storage.EastUS narrow the scope further.

scenario: A VM can't reach the internet, and you suspect a user-defined route is sending traffic somewhere unexpected. Which tool shows the next hop for traffic from the VM to a specific IP address?

options.note: Checks NSG rules, not routing.
Not a network diagnostic tool.
Don't show routing decisions.

explanation: Next hop shows the next hop type (Internet, VirtualAppliance, VirtualNetworkGateway, None, and so on), its IP, and the route table that decided it. Effective routes on the NIC show the full route list.

scenario: Traffic from a subnet to 10.50.0.0/16 must be dropped entirely. What should you add to the subnet's route table?

options.text: A route to 10.50.0.0/16 with next hop type None
A route to 10.50.0.0/16 with next hop type Internet
options.note: Sends the traffic to the internet.

options.text: A route with next hop type Virtual network
options.note: Keeps the traffic in the VNet.
Unrelated to routing.

explanation: Next hop type None drops the traffic. Other next hop types are Virtual network gateway, Virtual network, Internet and Virtual appliance.

scenario: Which statement about Standard SKU public IP addresses is correct?

options.text: They block inbound traffic unless an NSG allows it.

options.note: Standard public IPs are always static.
They can be zonal or zone-redundant.

options.text: They are open to all inbound traffic by default.
options.note: That was Basic SKU behavior; Basic is retired.

explanation: Standard public IPs are static and secure by default, and support availability zones. Basic SKU public IPs were retired in September 2025.

scenario: Your company bought the domain contoso.com from a third-party registrar. You create a public Azure DNS zone for contoso.com. What else must you do so Azure DNS answers queries for the domain?

options.text: Update the NS records at the registrar
Create a private DNS zone with the same name.
options.note: Private zones aren't resolvable from the internet.

options.text: Create an @ A record and a www CNAME in the zone
options.note: Records won't be found until the domain is delegated.

options.text: Link the zone to the virtual network hosting the web servers
options.note: Only private zones are linked to VNets.

explanation: Delegate the domain by setting the registrar's name server records to the four Azure DNS name servers shown on the zone. Azure DNS hosts zones but isn't a domain registrar.

scenario: You want www.contoso.com to point to the web app contoso-web.azurewebsites.net. Which DNS record type should you create?

options.note: An A record maps to an IP address.
For mail routing.
Used for verification, not aliasing.

explanation: A CNAME maps a name to another name. For the zone apex (contoso.com itself) you can't use a CNAME, but an Azure DNS alias record can point the apex at an Azure resource.

scenario: A private DNS zone corp.internal is linked to two VNets. VMs in VNet1 should get DNS records created automatically when they're deployed; VNet2 only needs to resolve names. How should the links be configured?

options.text: Enable auto-registration on the VNet1 link only.
Enable auto-registration on the VNet2 link only.
options.note: Works, but VNet2 only needs resolution.

options.text: Disable both links and use hosts files.
options.note: Defeats the purpose of private DNS.

options.text: Create a public zone for VNet2.
options.note: Public zones aren't for internal names.

explanation: A virtual network link can be a registration link (auto-registration on) or a resolution-only link. A VNet can have auto-registration enabled for only one private DNS zone.

scenario: VMs behind a public Standard Load Balancer need RDP access on port 3389, but only one VM should be reachable on frontend port 50001. What should you configure?

options.text: A load-balancing rule from port 50001 to 3389
options.note: Spreads RDP across all backends.
Controls outbound SNAT only.
Probes don't forward traffic.

explanation: Inbound NAT rules forward a specific frontend port to a specific backend VM and port. Azure Bastion is usually a more secure way to provide RDP access.

scenario: Two network virtual appliances behind an internal Standard Load Balancer must receive all TCP and UDP traffic on all ports, for high availability. What should you use?

options.text: One load-balancing rule per port (65,535 rules)
options.note: Impractical and exceeds limits.
Basic is retired and doesn't support HA ports.
Floating IP alone doesn't cover all ports.

explanation: HA ports (protocol All, port 0) on an internal Standard Load Balancer balances all flows on all ports. It's the standard pattern for active-active NVAs.

scenario: A load balancer health probe fails for every backend VM, so no traffic is forwarded. The app on the VMs is running. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the probe port is blocked
Whether each backend VM has its own public IP address
options.note: Backend VMs don't need public IPs.

options.text: Whether the storage account is GRS.
options.note: Unrelated.

options.text: Whether the VMs are in the same resource group.
options.note: Doesn't matter.

explanation: Probes come from 168.63.129.16 (the AzureLoadBalancer service tag). If an NSG or OS firewall blocks the probe port, or the probe path returns non-200 for HTTP probes, the backend is marked unhealthy.

scenario: One Application Gateway must send requests for /images/* to one backend pool and /video/* to another. What should you configure?

options.text: A path-based routing rule with a URL path map

options.note: Layer 4 load balancers can't route by URL path.
DNS-level only; can't see URL paths.
Keeps a user on one backend; no path routing.

explanation: Application Gateway is a layer 7 load balancer. Path-based rules route by URL path, and multi-site listeners route by host name. It also handles TLS termination and WAF.

scenario: A global web app runs in three regions. You need a single entry point that routes users to the closest healthy backend, caches static content at the edge, and includes WAF. What should you use?

options.note: Regional and layer 4.
Regional, not global.
Outbound only.

explanation: Front Door is a global layer 7 service with anycast entry, latency-based routing, health probes, caching (CDN) and WAF. Traffic Manager is a DNS-based global option without caching or layer 7 features.

scenario: You want DNS-based routing that sends all users to the primary region and fails over to a secondary region only if the primary is unhealthy, for a non-HTTP service. What should you use?

options.text: Traffic Manager with the Priority routing method

options.note: Splits traffic by weight; not primary/secondary.
Regional and HTTP only.
Front Door is designed for HTTP(S) traffic.

explanation: Traffic Manager works at the DNS level for any protocol. Its routing methods are Priority, Weighted, Performance, Geographic, Multivalue and Subnet.

scenario: Remote employees on laptops need to connect securely to an Azure VNet from home using their Microsoft Entra credentials. What should you configure?

options.text: A point-to-site VPN with Entra ID authentication
A site-to-site VPN to each employee's home router
options.note: Connects whole networks through a VPN device, not individual laptops.
Connects VNets, not remote clients.
A dedicated circuit for sites, not individual users.

explanation: Point-to-site VPN supports certificate, RADIUS and Microsoft Entra ID authentication (OpenVPN protocol). P2S requires a route-based gateway.

scenario: You need a site-to-site VPN plus point-to-site connections and multiple site-to-site tunnels. Which VPN type must the virtual network gateway use?

options.note: Supports only one S2S tunnel and no P2S.

options.text: Either; they support the same features
options.note: Policy-based has major limitations.
A different gateway type.

explanation: Route-based gateways support multiple S2S tunnels, P2S, VNet-to-VNet, BGP and coexistence with ExpressRoute. Policy-based gateways support one S2S tunnel with static policies.

scenario: When you create a VPN gateway, which subnet must exist in the VNet?

options.note: The name must be GatewaySubnet.
Reserved for Azure Firewall.
Gateways require GatewaySubnet.

explanation: VPN and ExpressRoute gateways deploy into GatewaySubnet. Microsoft recommends /27 or larger. Don't put other resources or NSGs on it.

scenario: You need a private, dedicated connection from your datacenter to Azure that doesn't go over the public internet, with predictable latency and up to 10 Gbps. What should you use?

options.note: Runs encrypted over the public internet.
For individual clients over the internet.
Connects Azure VNets only.

explanation: ExpressRoute provides a private connection through a connectivity provider. Private peering reaches VNets and Microsoft peering reaches Microsoft 365 and Azure public services. A site-to-site VPN can serve as a backup.

scenario: You deploy Azure Firewall to filter traffic for spoke VNets. Which subnet requirement applies?

options.note: Wrong name and too small.
Reserved for gateways.
Reserved for Bastion.

explanation: Azure Firewall needs a dedicated AzureFirewallSubnet of /26 or larger. Spoke subnets then use UDRs (0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall's private IP) to send traffic through it.

scenario: VMs must reach a storage account through the Azure backbone, and the storage firewall must allow only that subnet. You don't need a private IP for the storage account. What is the simplest option?

options.text: A service endpoint plus a storage firewall rule
Create a private endpoint and private DNS zone.
options.note: Also works, but adds a private IP and DNS setup you said you don't need.
Unnecessary.

options.text: Set public network access to 'Enabled from all networks'.
options.note: Allows everyone.

explanation: Service endpoints extend the subnet's identity to the service so its firewall can allow that subnet. The service keeps its public IP. They're free and simple; private endpoints are better when you need private IPs or on-premises access.

scenario: After creating a private endpoint for a storage account, VMs still connect to its public IP address. What is the most likely missing piece?

options.text: The privatelink private DNS zone and VNet link
An outbound NSG rule allowing 443 to the endpoint
options.note: Outbound 443 is allowed by default.

options.text: A public IP on the private endpoint.
options.note: Private endpoints don't use public IPs.
Unrelated.

explanation: Clients must resolve the storage FQDN to the private endpoint's IP. The privatelink private DNS zone, linked to the VNet, provides that record. On-premises clients need conditional forwarding, for example through Azure DNS Private Resolver.

scenario: On-premises DNS servers must resolve names in Azure private DNS zones, and Azure VMs must resolve on-premises names, without running DNS server VMs. What should you deploy?

options.note: Exposes internal names publicly.

options.text: Hosts files on every Azure VM and on-premises server
options.note: Unmanageable.
Global traffic routing, not DNS forwarding.

explanation: The inbound endpoint receives queries from on-premises (forward to its IP). The outbound endpoint with forwarding rulesets sends Azure queries for on-premises domains to your DNS servers.

scenario: A VM's NIC needs to forward traffic it receives for other destinations, because it runs firewall software. What must be enabled in Azure?

options.note: Improves performance; doesn't allow forwarding.
Not required for forwarding.
A load balancer setting.

explanation: By default Azure drops packets whose destination isn't the NIC's own IP. Enabling IP forwarding on the NIC (and inside the OS) lets the VM act as an NVA.

scenario: Which statement about NSG rule priority numbers for custom rules is correct?

options.text: Custom rules can use priorities 100–4096, and lower numbers are processed first.
Custom rules can use 1–65500, and higher numbers are processed first.
options.note: Wrong range and order.

options.text: All rules are evaluated, and Deny always wins.
options.note: Processing stops at the first match.

options.text: Priority only matters for outbound rules.
options.note: It applies to both directions.

explanation: Rules are processed from lowest to highest number until one matches. Two rules in the same direction can't share a priority number.

scenario: Users report intermittent failures connecting from a VM to an external API. You want to test TCP connectivity to api.contoso.com:443 from the VM and see where on the path it fails. Which Network Watcher tool is best for a one-time check?

options.note: Shows routing only.
Shows resource relationships only.
Shows NSG rules but doesn't test a connection.

explanation: Connection troubleshoot tests reachability from a VM (or other source) to a destination host and port. It reports latency, hops and issues like blocked NSG rules or DNS failures. Connection monitor does the same continuously.

scenario: Auditors need a record of who deleted resources in a subscription over the last 2 years. By default, how long are Activity log events kept, and what should you do?

options.text: 90 days; export it with a diagnostic setting

options.note: The platform keeps Activity log events for only 90 days.

options.text: 30 days; enable Azure Backup for the subscription
options.note: Backup doesn't protect logs, and the default is 90 days.
Events older than 90 days are removed.

explanation: The Activity log records control-plane operations (who did what, when) for 90 days. Export it with a diagnostic setting to Log Analytics, storage or Event Hubs to keep it longer and query it.

scenario: You need platform metrics for a VM going back more than 3 months for capacity planning. By default, how long does Azure Monitor keep platform metrics?

options.note: Longer than that.
Shorter than that.
Much longer than that.

explanation: Platform metrics are kept for 93 days. For longer history, send metrics to a Log Analytics workspace with a diagnostic setting (or a data collection rule for guest metrics) and set the retention you need.

scenario: A Log Analytics workspace keeps data for the default 30 days. Security wants query access to the last year of data. What should you change?

options.text: Create a second workspace and send data to both
options.note: Doesn't extend retention.
Covers only Activity log data.

options.text: Change the pricing tier to Free.
options.note: The Free tier has shorter retention and a daily cap.

explanation: Interactive retention can be set from 30 days up to 2 years per workspace or table. Long-term retention (archive) keeps data up to 12 years at lower cost, but needs search jobs or restore to query.

scenario: You need logs from an Azure SQL database and a Key Vault sent to a Log Analytics workspace. What do you configure on each resource?

options.text: The Azure Monitor Agent, installed through an extension
options.note: The agent runs on VMs, not on PaaS resources.
Defines alert notifications, not log collection.
Unrelated to logging.

explanation: Resource logs aren't collected by default. A diagnostic setting routes chosen log categories and metrics to Log Analytics, a storage account, Event Hubs or a partner solution. Azure Policy can deploy diagnostic settings at scale.

scenario: You want an email whenever anyone deletes a virtual machine in the production subscription. Which alert type should you create?

options.text: A metric alert on VM Availability dropping to 0
options.note: Metrics don't record deletions.

options.text: A log search alert on the Perf table
options.note: Perf holds performance counters, not management operations.
Tracks spending.

explanation: Activity log alerts fire on control-plane events (such as a delete operation), Service Health events and Resource Health events. Pair the alert with an action group that sends email.

scenario: You want to be notified when Azure has a service issue or planned maintenance affecting the regions and services your subscription uses. What should you configure?

options.text: A metric alert on every resource
options.note: Doesn't capture platform incidents.
Not real-time incident notifications.
Routes logs; doesn't send notifications on its own.

explanation: Service Health alerts (an Activity log alert type) notify you about service issues, planned maintenance, health advisories and security advisories for selected services and regions.

scenario: A single VM became unavailable, and you want to know whether an Azure platform problem caused it, along with its health history. Where should you look first?

options.note: Recommendations, not availability history.
Billing data.
Identity events.

explanation: Resource Health shows the current and past health of an individual resource and whether a platform event or a user action caused it. Service Health covers broader service and region incidents.

scenario: Nightly patching causes many CPU alerts between 01:00 and 03:00 on Sundays. Alerts should still fire and be recorded, but no notifications should be sent during that window. What should you configure?

options.text: An alert processing rule with a schedule
Delete the alert rules and recreate them on Monday
options.note: Error-prone, and alerts wouldn't be recorded.
Hides real problems all week.

options.text: Disable the Azure Monitor Agent during patching
options.note: Stops data collection.

explanation: Alert processing rules can suppress notifications or add action groups to fired alerts. They can be scoped to resources and limited to schedules such as maintenance windows.

scenario: You need an alert when a VM hasn't sent a heartbeat to Log Analytics for 10 minutes. Which alert type and table should you use?

options.text: A log search alert querying the Heartbeat table
An Activity log alert on VM stop
options.note: Misses OS hangs and agent failures where nothing is stopped.
Covers platform issues only.
Tracks spending.

explanation: The Azure Monitor Agent writes a Heartbeat record every minute. A log search alert can find computers whose latest heartbeat is older than a threshold. VM availability metrics are another option.

scenario: Which KQL query returns the latest heartbeat time for each computer?

options.text: SELECT Computer, MAX(TimeGenerated) FROM Heartbeat GROUP BY Computer
options.note: That's SQL, not KQL.
Not valid logic.
Returns one row overall, not one per computer.

explanation: summarize with an aggregation (max, count, avg) and 'by' groups results. arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by Computer would return the full latest row per computer.

scenario: You want to chart average CPU usage per computer in 5-minute bins over the last day. Which KQL operators complete this query?

options.note: project can't aggregate.
extend adds columns; take limits rows.
A self-join isn't needed.

explanation: bin() groups timestamps into fixed buckets, summarize aggregates within them, and render timechart draws the result.
code:
Perf
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ObjectName == "Processor" and CounterName == "% Processor Time"
| ...

scenario: Which table in a Log Analytics workspace holds Activity log records sent through a diagnostic setting?

options.note: Agent heartbeats.
Performance counters.
Windows event logs from agents.

explanation: Activity log data lands in AzureActivity. Other common tables are AzureDiagnostics or resource-specific tables for resource logs, Event and Syslog for OS logs, and Perf and InsightsMetrics for performance data.

scenario: You want a dependency map that shows the processes and connections between VMs, plus performance charts. What should you enable?

options.text: VM insights with the Map feature

options.note: Shows console output only.
Recommendations only.
Shows Azure resources, not processes and connections inside VMs.

explanation: VM insights uses the Azure Monitor Agent for performance data. Adding the Dependency agent enables the Map feature, which shows processes and network connections.

scenario: You need an interactive report that combines metrics, log queries and text for your operations team, and that they can parameterize by subscription. What should you create?

options.note: Sends notifications.
Defines data collection.
Routes logs.

explanation: Workbooks combine text, queries, metrics and parameters into interactive reports, and can be shared. Dashboards and Managed Grafana are alternatives for at-a-glance views.

scenario: NSG flow logs are being retired. Which feature should you use to log IP traffic flowing through a virtual network?

options.note: Control-plane operations only.
VM console output.
Application telemetry.

explanation: VNet flow logs record traffic at the VNet level, including encrypted traffic and more scenarios than NSG flow logs. New NSG flow logs can no longer be created, and existing ones retire in 2027. Traffic analytics can visualize flow logs.

scenario: You want to restore a single deleted file from last week's backup of an Azure VM without restoring the whole VM. What should you use?

options.text: Restore the full VM over the existing one
options.note: Overwrites current data.
No access to backups.
Replication for disaster recovery, not item-level restore.

explanation: File Recovery downloads a script that mounts the recovery point's disks as local volumes (over iSCSI). You browse and copy files, then unmount.

scenario: You need to back up Azure Blob storage, Azure Disks and Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers. Which vault type supports these workloads?

options.note: Recovery Services vaults handle VMs, SQL in VMs, Azure Files and MARS, not these.
Stores secrets and keys.
Not a backup vault.

explanation: Backup vaults support newer workloads such as Blobs, Disks, PostgreSQL and AKS. Recovery Services vaults support Azure VMs, SQL/SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files and on-premises backups with MARS or MABS.

scenario: You need to back up specific folders from an on-premises Windows file server directly to Azure, without System Center or a backup server. What should you install?

options.text: The Azure Monitor Agent, installed through an extension
options.note: Collects telemetry.
Syncs files; it isn't a backup with retention points.
Maps dependencies.

explanation: The MARS agent backs up files, folders and system state from Windows machines to a Recovery Services vault on a schedule.

scenario: A database VM needs backups every 4 hours. The standard VM backup policy allows only one backup per day. What should you use?

options.text: An Enhanced backup policy with an hourly schedule
Five standard policies on the same VM
options.note: A VM can have only one backup policy.
Applies to blobs.
Affects backup storage redundancy, not frequency.

explanation: Enhanced policies support multiple backups per day (every 4, 6, 8 or 12 hours), Trusted Launch VMs and more. Standard policies run once a day.

scenario: You want backups in a Recovery Services vault to be restorable in the paired region if the primary region is down. What should you configure, and when?

options.text: GRS and Cross Region Restore, before backups start
LRS with Cross Region Restore, at any time
options.note: CRR requires a GRS vault.

options.text: Copy the vault to another region manually.
options.note: Vaults can't be copied.
Soft delete protects against deletion, not regional outages.

explanation: Vault storage redundancy (LRS, ZRS or GRS) can only be changed before you configure backups. Cross Region Restore requires GRS and lets you restore in the secondary region at any time.

scenario: An attacker with admin access deletes backup data for several VMs. Which Azure Backup feature lets you recover the deleted backup data for a period after deletion?

options.text: Blob versioning on the vault's storage
options.note: Applies to storage accounts.
Protects the vault resource, not backup data inside it.
Doesn't recover deleted backups.

explanation: Backup soft delete keeps deleted backup data for 14 days by default, configurable up to 180 days. Newly created vaults have soft delete permanently enabled. Multi-user authorization and immutable vaults add further protection.

scenario: Before making changes to a VM, you start an on-demand backup. Where is the first recovery point stored for fast restores?

options.text: As a snapshot, then in the vault

options.note: Temporary disks aren't persistent.
Logs don't store data.
Stores logs, not backups.

explanation: VM backups first take snapshots, which are kept for a few days (configurable in the policy) for fast instant restores, then transfer the data to the vault for long-term retention.

scenario: You need disaster recovery for Azure VMs in East US with replication to West US, a target RPO of minutes, and the ability to test failover without affecting production. What should you use?

options.text: Azure Backup with GRS and Cross Region Restore
options.note: Daily backups give an RPO of up to 24 hours, and restoring takes longer.
Unmanaged storage replication doesn't orchestrate VM failover.
Connectivity only.

explanation: Site Recovery continuously replicates VMs to another region and orchestrates failover and failback. Test failover creates VMs in a separate network so production isn't affected.

scenario: During a regional outage, multiple VMs must fail over in a specific order (database first, then app tier, then web tier) with a script between steps. What should you create in Site Recovery?

options.text: Three replication policies with different RPOs
options.note: Doesn't control order.
Unrelated.
Backup isn't failover.

explanation: Recovery plans group VMs for ordered failover. They can include manual actions and Automation runbook scripts between groups.

scenario: You restore a VM from backup and want to keep the original VM running for comparison. Which restore option should you choose?

options.note: Overwrites the original VM's disks.
Recovers individual files only.
Not a restore option.

explanation: 'Create new' builds a new VM from the recovery point and 'Restore disks' gives you disks to attach or template from. 'Replace existing' swaps the disks of the current VM.

scenario: You need to see the pending OS updates for 200 Azure VMs and install critical updates every Saturday night. What should you use?

options.text: Azure Update Manager with a maintenance configuration

options.note: Retired with the Log Analytics agent; Update Manager replaces it.

options.text: The Custom Script Extension with a manual script
options.note: No assessment or compliance reporting.
Doesn't install patches.

explanation: Azure Update Manager assesses and installs updates for Azure and Arc-enabled machines without needing the retired Log Analytics agent. Maintenance configurations define the schedule, classifications and reboot behavior.

scenario: A VM-level alert should trigger an Azure Automation runbook that restarts a service. Where do you specify the runbook?

options.note: Severity is a label.
Defines collection only.

options.text: In the VM's boot diagnostics settings
options.note: Unrelated.

explanation: Action groups can run Automation runbooks, Azure Functions, Logic Apps, webhooks and ITSM actions, as well as sending notifications.

scenario: Monitoring must capture an application's custom text log file (C:\App\logs\*.log) from VMs into Log Analytics. What should you configure?

options.text: A DCR with a custom text log data source
A diagnostic setting on the VM resource
options.note: Platform diagnostic settings don't read files inside the guest OS.
Console output only.

options.text: Network Watcher packet capture on the VM
options.note: Captures network traffic.

explanation: The Azure Monitor Agent can collect custom text and JSON logs through a DCR, which defines the file pattern, the transformation and the destination table (a custom _CL table).

scenario: You enable self-service password reset (SSPR) for the group sspr-pilot and require two authentication methods. A Global Administrator in the pilot asks to use security questions as one of their methods. What happens?

options.text: Administrators can't use security questions; Microsoft Entra ID applies a stricter two-method policy to admin roles regardless of your SSPR settings.
Security questions work for admins if the tenant allows them for users.
options.note: Admin accounts follow the built-in two-gate policy, which excludes security questions.

options.text: Admins are excluded from SSPR and must call the help desk.
options.note: Admins have SSPR enabled by default; they just get a stricter policy.

options.text: The admin must be removed from sspr-pilot first.
options.note: Group scope applies to users; admin roles are always covered by their own policy.

explanation: Microsoft Entra ID always enables SSPR for administrator roles with a two-gate policy (two methods such as the Authenticator app, email or phone) and never allows security questions for them. Your SSPR settings for scope and methods apply to regular users.

scenario: Users created in on-premises AD DS and synchronized with Microsoft Entra Connect reset their passwords with SSPR, but they still can't sign in to their domain-joined PCs with the new password. What must you configure?

options.text: Password writeback in Microsoft Entra Connect (and enable it in SSPR settings)

options.note: Registration affects who can use SSPR, not where the new password is stored.
The number of methods doesn't change where the password is written.
Seamless SSO uses the on-premises password; it doesn't send cloud resets back to AD DS.

explanation: Without writeback, an SSPR reset only changes the cloud password. Password writeback (a Microsoft Entra ID P1 feature) sends the new password back to AD DS through Microsoft Entra Connect so on-premises sign-ins accept it.

scenario: Every member of the dynamic group Sales-All must receive a Microsoft 365 E3 license automatically, including people who join Sales later. What is the most efficient approach?

options.text: Assign the license to the Sales-All group (group-based licensing)
Assign the license to each user, and run a weekly script for new users
options.note: Works, but it's manual and misses users between runs.

options.text: Create an Azure Policy that assigns licenses
options.note: Azure Policy governs Azure resources, not Microsoft Entra licenses.

options.text: Add the license to the administrative unit that contains Sales
options.note: Administrative units delegate administration; they don't assign licenses.

explanation: Group-based licensing assigns licenses to everyone in a group, and adds or removes them as membership changes. Combined with a dynamic group, new Sales users are licensed automatically.

scenario: All new resources must carry the costCenter tag of the resource group they're created in. Teams often forget to add it. What should you do?

options.text: Assign the built-in Azure Policy "Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing" and create a remediation task for existing resources
Add the tag to each resource group; resources inherit it automatically
options.note: Resources don't inherit tags from their resource group.

options.text: Apply a CanNotDelete lock to each resource group
options.note: Locks prevent deletion; they don't add tags.

options.text: Use a Deny policy that blocks resources without tags
options.note: That stops deployments instead of adding the tag; the requirement is to carry the value automatically.

explanation: Tags aren't inherited. The built-in policy uses the Modify effect to copy the tag from the resource group at create or update time. A remediation task fixes resources that already exist.

scenario: Your organization wants to apply one Azure Policy to 40 subscriptions that belong to the finance department, and to any finance subscriptions created later. What should you use?

options.text: A management group that contains the finance subscriptions, with the policy assigned at that management group
A resource group in each subscription with the policy assigned there
options.note: Policy assigned to a resource group only covers that group.

options.text: A policy initiative assigned to each subscription individually
options.note: Initiatives group policies, but per-subscription assignment doesn't cover new subscriptions.

options.text: A tag on each subscription called department=finance
options.note: Tags don't carry policy assignments.

explanation: Policy and RBAC assignments at a management group are inherited by every subscription, resource group and resource beneath it, including subscriptions moved in later. A management group tree supports up to six levels below the root.

scenario: You gave a partner a service SAS URI for the container invoices. It was created from the stored access policy partner-read. The partner relationship has ended and access must stop immediately. What should you do?

options.text: Delete the stored access policy partner-read (or change its expiry to the past)
Delete the SAS URI from your records
options.note: The token stays valid; deleting your copy doesn't revoke it.
This also revokes access, but it breaks every other app and SAS that uses the keys.

options.text: Turn on soft delete for blobs
options.note: Soft delete protects data from deletion; it doesn't revoke access.

explanation: A stored access policy lets you revoke or change service SAS tokens on the server side. Up to five policies can exist per container. Without a policy, the only way to revoke a key-signed SAS is to rotate the key that signed it.

scenario: A developer wants to issue a user delegation SAS for a blob and manage its expiry through a stored access policy. Why won't this work?

options.text: Stored access policies only apply to service SAS tokens, not to user delegation SAS or account SAS
User delegation SAS tokens can't be used with blobs
options.note: User delegation SAS is a blob-only SAS type.

options.text: Stored access policies are only for Azure Files
options.note: They work for containers, file shares, queues and tables.

options.text: A user delegation SAS can only last one hour
options.note: It can last up to seven days.

explanation: A user delegation SAS is signed with Microsoft Entra credentials and a user delegation key, so it can't reference a stored access policy. To revoke it, revoke the user delegation key or remove the signer's permissions.

scenario: The storage account stlogs01 allows access only from selected networks. A Microsoft Fabric workspace must read data through its managed identity, and no other service of that type should get in. What should you configure?

options.text: A resource instance rule for that workspace in the storage account's networking settings
Enable "Allow Azure services on the trusted services list"
options.note: That admits trusted services broadly, not one specific instance.

options.text: Add the workspace's public IP addresses to the firewall
options.note: PaaS outbound IPs are shared and change; IP rules aren't meant for Azure services.
That removes the restriction for everyone.

explanation: Resource instance rules allow traffic from a specific Azure resource instance (identified by its resource ID and managed identity) through the storage firewall. The identity still needs an RBAC role such as Storage Blob Data Reader.

scenario: You need blobs written to a container in steastprod (East US) to be copied automatically to a container in stwestdr (West US). Which settings must be in place?

options.text: Object replication, with blob versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source account
Geo-redundant storage (GRS) on the source account
options.note: GRS replicates the whole account to the paired region; you can't pick the target account or container.

options.text: A lifecycle management rule that copies new blobs
options.note: Lifecycle rules tier or delete blobs; they don't copy them.

options.text: Blob soft delete on both accounts
options.note: Soft delete isn't a prerequisite for object replication.

explanation: Object replication asynchronously copies block blobs between containers in two accounts, which can be in different regions. It requires blob versioning on source and destination and change feed on the source.

scenario: Two departments share a storage account. Finance data must be encrypted with a customer-managed key in Key Vault, while Marketing data uses Microsoft-managed keys. What should you use?

options.text: Encryption scopes, with a customer-managed-key scope set as the default on the finance container
A second storage account is the only option
options.note: That works too, but encryption scopes solve it within one account.

options.text: Infrastructure encryption on the finance container
options.note: Infrastructure encryption is enabled for a whole account, at creation, and adds a second layer; it doesn't pick keys per container.
That encrypts VM disks, not blob containers.

explanation: Encryption scopes let you choose Microsoft-managed or customer-managed keys per container or per blob. A container can enforce its default scope so every blob in it uses that key.

scenario: A user deleted the file share projects in Azure Files four days ago. Soft delete for file shares was left at its default settings. What can you do?

options.text: Undelete the share from the storage account's File shares list (show deleted shares), because the default retention is 7 days
Nothing; deleted file shares can't be recovered
options.note: Share soft delete is on by default for new accounts.

options.text: Restore it from a blob version
options.note: Blob versioning doesn't cover Azure Files.

options.text: Open a support ticket to restore it from geo-redundant storage
options.note: GRS replicates deletions too; it isn't a backup.

explanation: Soft delete for Azure file shares is enabled by default with 7-day retention (configurable from 1 to 365 days). A soft-deleted share keeps its snapshots and can be undeleted during the retention period.

scenario: An app uses key1 of a storage account in its connection string. Security requires rotating the account keys without downtime. In what order should you work?

options.text: Switch the app to key2, regenerate key1, then later switch back to key1 and regenerate key2
Regenerate both keys at the same time, then update the app
options.note: The app fails between the regeneration and the update.

options.text: Regenerate key1 first, then update the app
options.note: The app fails as soon as key1 changes.

options.text: Disable shared key access, then re-enable it
options.note: This doesn't rotate anything and blocks key-based access in the meantime.

explanation: Storage accounts have two keys so you can rotate one while apps use the other. Better still, move apps to Microsoft Entra ID authorization and disallow shared key access entirely.

scenario: An administrator signs in to Azure Storage Explorer with a Microsoft Entra account that has the Contributor role on the storage account, but gets "authorization permission mismatch" when listing blobs with Entra authentication. What is missing?

options.text: A data-plane role such as Storage Blob Data Reader or Storage Blob Data Contributor
The Owner role on the subscription
options.note: Owner manages resources but still doesn't grant blob data access through Entra ID.
A SAS is a different way to authorize; the question is about Entra authentication.

options.text: Public network access set to "Enabled from all networks"
options.note: A network block returns a different error; this is a permission problem.

explanation: Contributor is a control-plane role: it can manage the account and read its keys, but Entra-based data access needs a Storage Blob Data role. Storage Explorer falls back to keys only if you choose that option.

scenario: You try to enable encryption at host on a new VM, but the option is unavailable. The VM size supports it. What should you check first?

options.text: That the EncryptionAtHost feature is registered for the Microsoft.Compute provider on the subscription
That Azure Disk Encryption is enabled first
options.note: It's the opposite: encryption at host can't be used on VMs that ever had Azure Disk Encryption.

options.text: That the VM uses an unmanaged disk
options.note: Encryption at host is for managed disks.

options.text: That the VM is in an availability set
options.note: Availability options are unrelated to this feature.

explanation: Encryption at host must be registered on the subscription (Register-AzProviderFeature -FeatureName EncryptionAtHost -ProviderNamespace Microsoft.Compute). It encrypts temp disks, caches and data flowing to storage. Existing VMs must be deallocated to turn it on.

scenario: A VM has used Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) for years. Security now wants end-to-end encryption including the temporary disk and disk caches, using encryption at host. What is true?

options.text: Encryption at host can't be enabled on a VM that currently has or ever had ADE; you need a new VM with new disks
Enable encryption at host while the VM is running
options.note: Even without ADE, existing VMs must be deallocated first.

options.text: Encryption at host and ADE can be layered on the same VM
options.note: Microsoft blocks this combination.

options.text: Disable ADE, then enable encryption at host on the same VM
options.note: A VM that ever had ADE isn't eligible.

explanation: Encryption at host and Azure Disk Encryption are mutually exclusive, including history: a VM that ever had ADE can't use encryption at host. Plan a migration to new disks on a new VM.

scenario: You need to move a running VM, its disks and its network resources from East US to Sweden Central with a guided process that checks dependencies. What should you use?

options.text: Move the VM to another resource group
options.note: Moving between resource groups doesn't change its region.
Resizing changes the VM size, not its region.

options.text: Export the resource group template and edit the location
options.note: Possible but manual; it doesn't move disks or data.

explanation: Azure Resource Mover moves resources across regions, identifies dependencies, and uses Azure Site Recovery replication for VMs. Moving between resource groups or subscriptions keeps the region and changes the resource ID.

scenario: A container app must pull images from a private Azure Container Registry without storing a password. What is the recommended setup?

options.text: Give the container app a managed identity and assign it the AcrPull role on the registry
Enable the registry's admin user and store its password as a secret
options.note: This works, but it uses a shared password, which Microsoft discourages.
This exposes images to everyone.

options.text: Assign the container app the Contributor role on the registry
options.note: Contributor is far more than needed; AcrPull is the least-privilege role.

explanation: Managed identities with the AcrPull role avoid credentials entirely. The same pattern works for Container Instances, App Service and AKS.

scenario: You want to send 10% of traffic to a new version of a container app and 90% to the current version, then shift traffic gradually. What must you configure?

options.text: Multiple revision mode, then set traffic weights on the two revisions
Single revision mode with two replicas
options.note: Single revision mode runs one active revision; replicas are copies of the same revision.

options.text: A second container app behind the same ingress
options.note: Container Apps does this natively with revisions.
Slots are an App Service feature, not Container Apps.

explanation: Each change to a container app's template creates a revision. In multiple revision mode, several revisions can be active and ingress splits traffic between them by percentage.

scenario: A nightly data job runs in Azure Container Instances. It should be restarted only if it exits with an error, and must stop after it succeeds. Which restart policy should you set?

options.note: The default; it restarts even after success, so the job would run endlessly.
It won't retry a failed run.
Not an ACI restart policy.

explanation: Container Instances supports Always (default, for long-running services), OnFailure (retry tasks that fail) and Never (run once). CPU and memory are set per container when you create the container group.

scenario: You need to back up an App Service app every 2 hours, keep backups for 90 days, and store them in your own storage account. The app runs on a Standard plan. What should you configure?

options.text: A custom backup schedule that points to a storage account container
Automatic backups; they meet these requirements by default
options.note: Automatic backups are hourly with 30-day retention that you can't change.
Slots stage releases; they aren't backups.

options.text: Upgrade to Premium because Standard can't back up
options.note: Basic, Standard, Premium and Isolated all support backups.

explanation: App Service has automatic backups (hourly, 30 days, no storage account needed) and custom backups (configurable schedule and retention, written to a storage account through SAS). Custom backups are limited to 10 GB.

scenario: You want to map www.contoso.com to an App Service app and secure it with a free certificate. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Add a CNAME record to the app's default host name and an asuid.www TXT record for verification, then create a free App Service managed certificate
A free managed certificate can cover *.contoso.com
options.note: Managed certificates don't support wildcard names.

options.text: Custom domains work on the Free (F1) tier with a managed certificate
options.note: Managed certificates and TLS bindings need a paid tier (Basic or higher).

options.text: Only an A record is needed, and the certificate is created automatically
options.note: A records are for root (apex) domains, and you must create the certificate and binding.

explanation: App Service verifies domain ownership with a TXT record named asuid.<subdomain> containing the app's verification ID. Free managed certificates renew automatically but can't be wildcard or exported. Use a purchased or Key Vault certificate for those cases.

scenario: Before swapping a staging slot into production, you need the production slot to keep its own database connection string. What should you do?

options.text: Mark the connection string as a deployment slot setting in each slot
Store the connection string in the code
options.note: It would swap with the code.
Auto swap triggers swaps automatically; it doesn't keep settings in place.
Instance count doesn't affect which settings swap.

explanation: App settings and connection strings swap with the slot unless they're marked as deployment slot settings ("sticky"). Sticky settings stay with the slot, so production keeps its production values.

scenario: Your team has an ARM template JSON file and wants to maintain it in Bicep from now on. Which command creates a starting Bicep file?

options.note: build compiles Bicep into ARM JSON, the opposite direction.
Not a real conversion command; export works on existing resource groups.
az group create makes resource groups; it doesn't convert templates.

explanation: az bicep decompile converts ARM JSON to Bicep on a best-effort basis; review the output and fix any warnings. To capture deployed resources, export the resource group as a template, then decompile it.

scenario: You're creating a new scale set that must mix VM sizes and include Spot VMs, and you want to manage instances with standard VM operations. Which orchestration mode should you choose?

options.note: Uniform uses one identical VM model, which suits large stateless fleets.
Availability sets don't scale automatically.
It controls physical closeness, not orchestration.

explanation: Flexible orchestration, recommended for most new scale sets, supports mixed sizes, Spot and regular VMs, and standard VM APIs. Uniform mode manages identical instances through the scale set model.

scenario: A VM's subnet has an NSG that allows inbound TCP 443 from the internet. The VM's NIC has another NSG with only the default rules. Can clients reach the VM on port 443?

options.text: No; inbound traffic must be allowed by both the subnet NSG and the NIC NSG, and the NIC's default rules deny it
Yes, because the subnet NSG is evaluated last and wins
options.note: For inbound traffic the subnet NSG is evaluated first, then the NIC NSG; both must allow it.

options.text: Yes, because NIC NSGs only filter outbound traffic
options.note: NSGs on NICs filter both directions.

options.text: Only if the VM has a Standard SKU public IP
options.note: The SKU doesn't override NSG rules.

explanation: For inbound traffic Azure applies the subnet NSG and then the NIC NSG; for outbound, the NIC NSG and then the subnet NSG. Use the NIC's Effective security rules view (the VM must be running) to see the combined result.

scenario: Admins must connect to VMs through Azure Bastion using the native SSH and RDP clients on their workstations (az network bastion ssh/rdp), not the browser. Which Bastion configuration supports this?

options.text: Standard or Premium SKU with native client support enabled

options.note: Developer is a free browser-only option for dev/test.
Basic doesn't support native client connections.

options.text: Any SKU, as long as the VMs have public IPs
options.note: Bastion exists so VMs don't need public IPs; native client needs Standard or higher.

explanation: Native client support, shareable links and IP-based connections need the Standard SKU (Premium adds features such as session recording). Bastion needs a subnet named AzureBastionSubnet of /26 or larger.

scenario: Two backend VMs behind a Standard internal load balancer show as unhealthy, although the app responds locally on port 8080. The NSG has a custom rule DenyAllInbound at priority 4000. What is the likely cause?

options.text: The custom deny rule overrides the default AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound rule, so the health probe is blocked
Standard load balancers don't support health probes on port 8080
options.note: Probes can use any TCP or HTTP port.

options.text: The VMs need public IP addresses for probes
options.note: Probes come from the platform address 168.63.129.16, not over the internet.

options.text: Health probes only work with Basic load balancers
options.note: Basic load balancers were retired in 2025; Standard uses probes normally.

explanation: Health probes come from 168.63.129.16, matched by the AzureLoadBalancer service tag. The default rule that allows them has priority 65001, so any custom deny with a lower number blocks probes. Add an allow rule for AzureLoadBalancer above your deny rule.

scenario: VMs in snet-app must reach a storage account over the Azure backbone. The storage account can keep its public endpoint, but only that subnet should be allowed, with no extra IP addresses to manage. What should you configure?

options.text: A Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on snet-app, plus a virtual network rule in the storage firewall
A private endpoint and a private DNS zone
options.note: Also secure, but it adds a private IP and DNS; a service endpoint meets the requirement more simply.

options.text: A NAT gateway on the subnet
options.note: It controls outbound internet IPs; it doesn't restrict the storage account to the subnet.

options.text: A user-defined route to the Internet next hop
options.note: Routing to Internet doesn't authorize the subnet at the storage firewall.

explanation: Service endpoints extend the subnet's identity to the PaaS service over the backbone while traffic still targets the public endpoint. Private endpoints give the service a private IP in your VNet and are required when traffic must stay private end to end or come from on-premises.

scenario: You must back up Azure managed disks with incremental snapshots, and blobs with operational backup. Which vault type do you create?

options.note: Recovery Services vaults hold backups for VMs, Azure Files, SQL/SAP HANA in VMs and on-premises (MARS/MABS).
Key Vault stores secrets, keys and certificates, not backups.

options.text: A storage account with soft delete
options.note: Soft delete helps, but it isn't Azure Backup.

explanation: Azure Backup uses two vault types. Backup vaults serve newer workloads such as Azure Disk Backup, Azure Blob backup, Azure Database for PostgreSQL and AKS. Recovery Services vaults serve Azure VMs, Azure Files and workloads inside VMs.

scenario: Management wants weekly reports of backup jobs, storage used and policy compliance across 12 vaults. What must you configure first?

options.text: Diagnostic settings on each vault that send backup data to a Log Analytics workspace, then use Backup Reports
An action group with an email receiver
options.note: Action groups send alerts, not reports.

options.text: Cross Region Restore on each vault
options.note: It enables restores in the paired region; it doesn't produce reports.
Lifecycle policies tier or delete blobs; they don't report on backups.

explanation: Backup Reports (in Business Continuity Center or Backup center) read from Log Analytics. Send each vault's diagnostics to a workspace, preferably in resource-specific mode. For failures, use the built-in Azure Monitor alerts for Azure Backup.

scenario: You replicate a production VM to another region with Azure Site Recovery. You must prove that failover works without affecting production or replication. What should you do?

options.text: Run a test failover into an isolated virtual network, then clean up the test failover
Run an unplanned failover to the production VNet
options.note: A real failover disrupts production.

options.text: Stop replication and restore from backup
options.note: This breaks protection and doesn't test Site Recovery.

options.text: Run a planned failover during business hours
options.note: A planned failover still moves production.

explanation: Test failover creates VMs from replicated data in a network you choose (ideally isolated) while replication continues. After validating, run Cleanup test failover to delete the test resources.

scenario: After a real Site Recovery failover to the secondary region, the VMs are running and confirmed healthy. What are the next steps to get protection and a way back?

options.text: Commit the failover, then re-protect the VMs so they replicate back to the primary region

options.note: You need them, or the primary region, for failback.
Testing doesn't restore replication.
This removes protection entirely.

explanation: Commit finalizes the failover and removes other recovery points. Re-protect starts replication from the secondary back to the primary, so you can later fail back with a planned failover.

scenario: Every Saturday from 1 AM to 5 AM you patch servers, and alerts fire during the window. Alert rules should still evaluate, but no one should be notified then. What should you create?

options.text: An alert processing rule with a recurring schedule that suppresses notifications
Delete the alert rules and recreate them each week
options.note: Manual and error-prone.
You'd miss alerts outside the window too.

options.text: Raise the severity of the alerts
options.note: Severity doesn't stop notifications.

explanation: Alert processing rules modify fired alerts at scale: suppress action groups during maintenance windows, or add action groups to many alert rules at once, filtered by scope, resource type or severity.

scenario: You need to continuously measure reachability, latency and packet loss between Azure VMs and an on-premises server, and be alerted when it degrades. Which tool fits?

options.text: Connection monitor in Azure Network Watcher

options.note: IP flow verify tests one packet against NSG rules at a point in time.
It shows the next routing hop, not ongoing performance.
Flow logs record traffic; they don't measure latency between endpoints.

explanation: Connection monitor runs scheduled tests between Azure VMs, scale sets, on-premises machines (through Azure Arc and Azure Monitor Agent) and URLs, and records reachability, round-trip time and loss with alerting.

scenario: You need VM insights performance charts and the dependency map for 30 VMs. What do the VMs need?

options.text: The Azure Monitor Agent with a VM insights data collection rule (and the Dependency agent for the map)

options.note: Boot diagnostics captures console screenshots and logs only.
MMA was retired in August 2024.

options.text: Network Watcher enabled in the region
options.note: Network Watcher doesn't collect guest performance data.

explanation: VM insights collects guest performance through Azure Monitor Agent and a data collection rule into Log Analytics. The Map feature also needs the Dependency agent. Enable it from Monitor > Insights > Virtual machines or with Azure Policy at scale.
